# Agent instructions

Coding agents follow the same rules as human contributors: read [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) and [ARCHITECTURE.md](ARCHITECTURE.md) before changing code.

Verification, from the repository root:

```
./gradlew test :cli:installDist :cli:distZip
```

Invariants: fail closed; never initialize target classes or invoke their code (the only JVM that sees them is the link-check worker, which links rewritten classes for the verifier without initializing them); behavior stays `NOT_VERIFIED`; do not change report schemas incompatibly; never commit private or third-party binaries.

```

`ARCHITECTURE.md`:

```md
# Architecture

ClassRevive turns compiled Java (`.class`, `.jar`, Android APK/dex, executables with an embedded jar) into readable source and measures how much of it is right. It runs several decompilers, recompiles their output, compares the result with the original bytecode, and keeps, file by file and method by method, what the evidence supports. This page describes how that is built. Commands and options are in the [command-line reference](docs/cli-reference.md); report fields are in [docs/reports.md](docs/reports.md).

## Principles

- **The target is data.** ClassRevive never initializes a target class, never invokes a target method or constructor and never executes a target program. Bytecode is read with ASM. The only place target-derived classes enter a JVM is the link check: after bytecode is rewritten (an obfuscator reversal, a whole-jar pass, a failure-lab reduction), a worker JVM defines the classes in an isolated class loader and links them so the JVM bytecode verifier checks them, without initializing them. A few passes evaluate pure constant code of the target (string and number decoders of known obfuscators, integer folds) in a bounded static interpreter written for that purpose, with an explicit instruction allowlist and step and memory budgets; the interpreter does not define classes or call target methods.
- **Fail closed.** Inputs that cannot be handled safely (unsafe archive names, identity/path mismatches, signed jars for rewriting passes, unsupported class versions) are refused with a diagnostic instead of being guessed at. Output folders must be new; nothing is overwritten.
- **Evidence over claims.** Every result says what was measured: recompilation, structural signatures, per-method round trip. Behavior is always `NOT_VERIFIED`. A compiled candidate is not called equivalent to the original.
- **Bounded everything.** Input size, expanded size, entry counts, worker time, heap, log and output sizes, search attempts and interpreter steps all have limits, and hitting one is reported.

## Modules

The build has 17 Gradle modules under `modules/`. Arrows point to what a module depends on.

| Module | Role |
|---|---|
| `model` | Immutable inventory types: `ClassInfo`, `MemberInfo`, `Inventory`, `Diagnostic`, `Limits` |
| `bytecode` | ASM-based readers: class inspection, readable bytecode fallback, dynamic-linkage scan, obfuscation profile and classifier, compiler fingerprint, reference index and call hierarchy, stub synthesis, class reduction, a JVM link check worker |
| `intake` | Bounded archive and class reading (`InventoryReader`), multi-release handling → `model`, `bytecode` |
| `engine-spi` | The decompiler engine interface, `ProcessRunner` (worker JVMs) and worker concurrency limits |
| `engine-cfr`, `engine-vineflower`, `engine-procyon`, `engine-jadx` | One adapter per decompiler, each run in its own worker JVM → `engine-spi` |
| `dex` | Dalvik conversion through dex2jar in a worker, and normalization of the converted classes → `engine-spi` |
| `transforms` | Bytecode passes (integer and string folds, static string decoder, ZKM flags), class-set renaming and mapping import, and the Skidfuscator and Aidsfuscator reversals (`transforms/skid`) → `engine-spi` |
| `verification` | javac workers, structural signature coverage, per-method round trip, source repairs, method splicing, placeholder typing → `bytecode`, `intake` |
| `selection` | Candidate ranking, hybrids, repairs, swaps and composition (`SourceSelector`) → `verification` |
| `sandbox` | Probe, policy and comparison model for future behavioral verification; no target execution |
| `pipeline` | The jobs: decompile, diagnose, transform, rename, benchmark, failure lab, reference comparison; input identification, native triage, reports and project export → everything above |
| `workbench` | Application layer shared by the front ends: decompile service, engine registry, result index, obfuscation check, reversal, native triage → `pipeline` |
| `gui` | Desktop application (Swing, FlatLaf, RSyntaxTextArea) → `workbench` |
| `cli` | The `classrevive` command line and the distribution (`installDist`, `distZip`, launchers `classrevive` and `classrevive-gui`) → `pipeline`, `workbench`, `gui` |

## Worker isolation

Everything that runs third-party or heavy code on target-derived data runs in a separate JVM started by `ProcessRunner`: each decompiler, javac, the transform and rename workers, the dex2jar conversion, the bytecode fallback, the diagnostics scan and the link check. A worker gets:

- the running JDK's `java`, an explicit class path, and an environment with `JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS`, `_JAVA_OPTIONS` and `JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS` removed, so injected JVM flags are not inherited;
- a wall-clock timeout, a heap and metaspace limit (decompiler heaps are sized by the input, up to 1 GiB), a retained-log limit and an output budget measured while it runs;
- a fixed protocol: inputs and outputs are files in the job folder, read back strictly by the parent.

Worker JVMs are fault isolation, **not an operating-system sandbox**. For deliberately hostile files, run ClassRevive in an isolated VM.

dex2jar runs with its own class path (`lib/dex2jar`), apart from the application's, because it bundles its own copy of ASM and Android's `dx`.

## The decompile flow

1. **Intake.** The input is read once under the intake limits (256 MiB input, 16 MiB per expanded entry, 512 MiB expanded in total, 20,000 entries). Entries are never extracted or executed; nested jars are resources. An input that is not a class or jar is identified from its bytes: an executable with an embedded jar, a bundle of jars, an Android APK or dex, or something without Java to take, which is reported and refused.
2. **Normalization.** Android inputs are converted to class files by dex2jar and normalized for Java decompilers. Class names that collide by letter case or are no Java identifiers, and private members with non-identifier names, get portable names in the rename worker, with the mapping kept. Multi-release jars are decompiled at their base version. The result is `classes.jar`, class files only.
3. **Diagnosis and reversal.** The static obfuscation profile is built from the original classes ([docs/obfuscation-detection.md](docs/obfuscation-detection.md)). A Skidfuscator or Aidsfuscator diagnosis with `HIGH` confidence runs that reversal first; ZKM flag accessors trigger the flag fold. Reversed classes must pass the JVM verifier in a fresh JVM (linked, never initialized) or the originals are kept. From here on everything is measured against the classes the engines read.
4. **Engines.** CFR, Vineflower, Procyon and JADX (any subset) run concurrently, two to four at a time depending on the processor count. For Android inputs JADX may read the original dex files instead. Engine outputs can be cached by input and engine bytes.
5. **Verification.** Each engine tree is compiled by javac in a worker with `-proc:none`, `-implicit:none`, an always-empty source path and either an empty class path or the explicit `--classpath` jars (normalized, base versions only). Original classes are never on that class path, so they cannot hide missing sources. Types nobody supplies get inferred stand-ins on the compiler's class path only, and such results are marked stub-backed. JADX's placeholder types are typed from javac's attribution before compiling. Structural signatures (class hierarchy, relevant modifiers, field and method names and descriptors) are compared with the original, and every recompiled method body is compared with the original bytecode after normalizations for javac variations and decompiler rewritings that keep JVM semantics.
6. **Selection.** See below.
7. **Fallback and reports.** When recovery is partial, an ASM dump of the original instructions is kept. `report.txt`, `report.json` (schema v1) and a self-contained `report.html` record inputs and their hashes, engine outcomes, every attempt and the provenance of each selected file and method; `project/` is an IDE project of the result.

## Selection and composition

Selection is a bounded, deterministic search, not an exhaustive optimum.

- **Ranking.** Candidates are ordered by complete compilation and signature coverage, compilation status, fully covered classes, average per-class coverage (each class weighs the same), matched signatures, whether javac got past parsing, error count, then the per-method round trip, then placeholder signals. Ties keep the first engine in lexical order.
- **Hybrids.** When no engine tree passes, up to eight hybrids replace failing files with another engine's version of the same file, guided by javac's per-file errors. Files holding a nested-class family move together, and a family is never mixed between nested and top-level forms.
- **Fill.** Classes an engine left empty or missing are filled in from the engine whose version of that file has the fewest errors.
- **Source repairs.** Up to three rounds of compiler-guided edits inside method bodies (casts, type arguments, `final` locals, renamed locals, guarded initializers, boolean literals, unreachable jumps). Declarations are never edited, and an edit is kept only when its file's errors drop and no class loses a signature. Files that still fail are swapped for other engines' versions.
- **Per-method composition.** A method body that does not compile, or whose round trip is `DIFFERENT`, can be replaced by the same method from another engine. The replacement is kept only when its file compiles alone against the original classes, every name in the copied body resolves to the same declaration, and the method's round trip becomes identical or equivalent with no other method of the file getting worse. Imports, fields and declarations are never copied. This is the one place where the original classes are on javac's class path, in memory and only to measure; the selection verdict always comes from a normal attempt without them.

`selection/selection.txt` and `report.json` list every attempt, edit, replacement and refusal.

## Transforms

`transform` and `rename` are separate commands that write a new jar plus audit evidence; `decompile` applies some of them by itself as described above.

- **Pass pipeline.** Built-in passes are registered explicitly and run in a fixed order inside a worker, with change and time budgets ([docs/pass-sdk.md](docs/pass-sdk.md)). Folds never cross labels, frames or debug boundaries; a folded branch removes dead code only up to the next stack map frame, so the output passes the JVM verifier.
- **Static string decoder.** Evaluates same-class static `(String)String` decoders with an allowlist of instructions and JDK calls, step, allocation and output budgets. Unsupported shapes are left unchanged. Decoded values never appear in the audit.
- **Obfuscator reversals.** The Skidfuscator and Aidsfuscator reversals are whole-jar passes: they recover the keys and seeds these tools compute, fold their opaque predicates and flattening, decrypt strings and numbers with a bounded interpreter of the tool's own decryptors, and remove the generated helper classes. They were written by reading the bytecode these tools emit; no code of the tools is copied. Frames are recomputed with a class hierarchy built from the input itself; only JDK classes are looked up, through the platform class loader, never a class of the input.
- **Renaming.** Deterministic aliases, explicit mapping files or an imported ProGuard/R8 mapping, applied to class sets, private members, manifests, `META-INF/services` and literal reflection calls, with forward and inverse maps in `rename.json`. Only what can be applied safely is applied; every skip is counted with its reason.

## Diagnostics and native code

`diagnose` reports static invokedynamic, reflection, class-loading and crypto references (clues, never verdicts), the obfuscation profile and the compiler fingerprint. With `--native`, bundled native libraries are extracted as data and triaged: ClassRevive reads their headers itself, and an external Ghidra the user installed can analyze them headless in its own process. Native code is never loaded or run.

## Desktop application

The `gui` module is a Swing application with FlatLaf and RSyntaxTextArea. It calls the pipeline only through `workbench`, the same layer the CLI uses for decompiling, so both front ends write the same result folders. Long work runs off the event thread with progress and cancellation. The explorer shows the inventory and bytecode before any decompile; after one, each class carries its confidence level, each method its round-trip mark, and javac errors are underlined. Find usages and the call hierarchy come from an index of the bytecode built in the background with ASM. Results live under a workspace folder (`%APPDATA%\ClassRevive\workspaces` on Windows, `~/.classrevive/workspaces` elsewhere) and can be reopened. The interface is translated into English and Portuguese (`messages*.properties`), and the distribution's `docs/guia-iniciante.md` is opened from the Help menu.

## Measuring

- `./gradlew test` runs unit and integration tests on fixtures the tests generate, plus the committed regression cases in `benchmarks/regressions/`.
- `benchmark` measures any corpus per engine and combined; `./gradlew :cli:scoreboard` runs it on real libraries from Maven Central, hash-checked by `gradle/verification-metadata.xml` (`dev` is measured while developing; no rule was tuned on the `holdout` and `holdout2` sets).
- The failure lab (`lab`, `lab-minimize`, `lab-promote`, `lab-check`) captures each failure with a signature that names no target content, minimizes it with ASM under the JVM verifier, and promotes license-compatible cases to permanent regressions.
- `compare-reference` scores a decompile of an obfuscated jar against the original jar, for answer-key corpora such as `benchmarks/obfuscated/`.

## Known limits

- javac runs on JDK 21, so recompilation covers Java 1.1 to 21 class files; newer ones are reported as `UNSUPPORTED_RELEASE`. ASM parses class files through Java 28 for everything else.
- Dependencies are never downloaded; without the real libraries, external types are stand-ins and signatures are checked against guesses.
- Generic signatures, annotations and constant values are not compared, and method-body behavior is not verified.
- Placeholder detection is a text heuristic over the stub text the engines emit.
- Reflection through variables, names renamed by an obfuscator without a mapping, and code generated at run time are out of reach of static analysis.

```

`CHANGELOG.md`:

```md
# Changelog

All notable changes to ClassRevive are listed here. The format follows [Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com/en/1.1.0/), and versions follow [Semantic Versioning](https://semver.org/). Before 1.0.0, minor versions may change command options and report fields; report schema changes stay additive within `schema_version` 1.

## [0.1.0] - 2026-10-31

First public release. Requires a Java 21 JDK.

ClassRevive is released under its own permissive license, the ClassRevive License 1.0 (`LICENSE`): commercial use, modification and redistribution with credit; the name and visual identity stay with the project. Bundled libraries keep their own licenses (`third-party-licenses/`).

### Engines and selection

- CFR 0.152, Vineflower 1.11.1, Procyon 0.6.0 and JADX 1.5.3, each in its own worker JVM with time, heap, log and output budgets and stable outcome codes; `--engines` picks any subset, and engine outputs can be cached (`--engine-cache`).
- Every candidate is recompiled by javac in a worker and measured: structural signature coverage per class, and a per-method round trip of each recompiled body against the original bytecode, with normalizations for javac variations and decompiler rewritings that keep JVM semantics.
- Deterministic ranking, bounded hybrids guided by javac's per-file errors, filling of classes an engine left empty or missing, compiler-guided source repairs, swaps after repair, and per-method composition that takes a body from another engine only when it compiles and its round trip is identical or equivalent.
- Inferred stand-ins for types no input or `--classpath` jar supplies, on the compiler's class path only; such results are marked stub-backed.
- Readable ASM fallback of the original instructions when recovery is partial.
- Compiler idioms undone in the selected sources, guided by the original bytecode and kept only when the file still compiles and its round trip does not get worse: enum switches lowered to switch maps or `ordinal()`, synthetic `access$` accessors and similar lowered forms.

### Inputs

- `.class` and `.jar` inputs, multi-release jars (decompiled at their base version, variants listed), several inputs or a folder per run.
- Portable names for classes that collide by letter case or are no Java identifiers, and for private members with non-identifier names, applied before the engines with the mapping kept.
- `identify`: executables, installers, native images and archives recognized from their bytes; a jar embedded in an executable, or the main jar of a bundle of jars, is extracted as data and decompiled.
- Android APK and dex inputs converted by dex2jar in a worker and normalized for Java decompilers; JADX can read the original dex; a local Android SDK is used when present; `AndroidManifest.xml` decoded and summarized.

### Deobfuscation

- Static obfuscation profile and obfuscator hypotheses with scores and reasons (Zelix KlassMaster, Allatori, Stringer, DashO, ProGuard/R8, native layers, Skidfuscator, Aidsfuscator), documented in `docs/obfuscation-detection.md`.
- Skidfuscator and Aidsfuscator reversals as whole-jar passes, checked by the JVM verifier without initializing classes; `decompile` applies them automatically on a `HIGH` diagnosis (`--deobfuscate auto|off`).
- ZKM opaque-predicate flags proved constant over the whole jar are folded before the engines.
- Opt-in bounded passes: integer constant, unary and branch folding, adjacent string operations, and a static decoder for pure `(String)String` methods.

### Renaming

- `rename`: deterministic aliases, explicit mapping files or an imported ProGuard/R8 mapping, applied to class sets, private members, manifests, `META-INF/services` and literal reflection calls, with forward and inverse maps and per-reason skip evidence.

### Diagnostics

- `diagnose`: static invokedynamic, reflection, class-loading and crypto references as clues, compiler fingerprint (javac with a version lower bound, ecj, Kotlin, Scala, Groovy) and embedded library recognition.
- Optional `--native` triage of bundled native libraries, with an external Ghidra when the user has one.

### Reports

- `report.txt`, `report.json` (schema v1), a self-contained `report.html` confidence map per class, and an IDE project export (`project/`).
- `compare-reference` scores a decompile against an original jar, for answer-key corpora.

### Desktop application

- `classrevive-gui` (or `classrevive gui`): open or drop a file, browse packages, classes, resources and bytecode, decompile with progress and cancellation, read the selected source or any engine's version, per-class confidence and per-method round-trip marks, javac errors underlined, side-by-side engine comparison, obfuscator banner with reversal, find usages and call hierarchy, go to class, code search, export as a project or a zip, dark and light themes, English and Portuguese.

### Measurement

- `benchmark` with per-engine and combined variants, separate compilation, structural and round-trip metrics, and per-file partial credit reported apart.
- Scoreboard on hash-checked Maven Central libraries (`./gradlew :cli:scoreboard`, sets `dev`, `holdout`, `holdout2`).
- Failure lab: capture, ASM minimization under the JVM verifier, promotion to permanent regression cases checked by `./gradlew test`.

### Documentation

- README in English and Brazilian Portuguese, a getting-started guide in both languages, a command-line reference, a benchmarks page with the measured scoreboard and how to reproduce it, a security policy and a disclaimer on responsible use.

### Platforms

- Builds and tests pass on Linux, macOS and Windows in CI. Paths through system symbolic links (such as macOS temporary folders) are accepted; links inside inputs and outputs are still refused.

### Safety

- Target code is never run: no target class is initialized and no target method is invoked. Rewritten classes are only linked, in a worker JVM, so the JVM verifier can check them. Worker JVMs drop injected JVM options. Worker isolation is fault containment, not an operating-system sandbox.
- Bounded intake (256 MiB input, 16 MiB per entry, 512 MiB expanded, 20,000 entries); dependencies are never downloaded.

```

`CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md`:

```md
# Contributor Covenant Code of Conduct

## Our Pledge

We as members, contributors, and leaders pledge to make participation in our community a harassment-free experience for everyone, regardless of age, body size, visible or invisible disability, ethnicity, sex characteristics, gender identity and expression, level of experience, education, socio-economic status, nationality, personal appearance, race, caste, color, religion, or sexual identity and orientation.

We pledge to act and interact in ways that contribute to an open, welcoming, diverse, inclusive, and healthy community.

## Our Standards

Examples of behavior that contributes to a positive environment for our community include:

* Demonstrating empathy and kindness toward other people
* Being respectful of differing opinions, viewpoints, and experiences
* Giving and gracefully accepting constructive feedback
* Accepting responsibility and apologizing to those affected by our mistakes, and learning from the experience
* Focusing on what is best not just for us as individuals, but for the overall community

Examples of unacceptable behavior include:

* The use of sexualized language or imagery, and sexual attention or advances of any kind
* Trolling, insulting or derogatory comments, and personal or political attacks
* Public or private harassment
* Publishing others' private information, such as a physical or email address, without their explicit permission
* Other conduct which could reasonably be considered inappropriate in a professional setting

## Enforcement Responsibilities

Community leaders are responsible for clarifying and enforcing our standards of acceptable behavior and will take appropriate and fair corrective action in response to any behavior that they deem inappropriate, threatening, offensive, or harmful.

Community leaders have the right and responsibility to remove, edit, or reject comments, commits, code, wiki edits, issues, and other contributions that are not aligned to this Code of Conduct, and will communicate reasons for moderation decisions when appropriate.

## Scope

This Code of Conduct applies within all community spaces, and also applies when an individual is officially representing the community in public spaces. Examples of representing our community include using an official e-mail address, posting via an official social media account, or acting as an appointed representative at an online or offline event.

## Enforcement

Instances of abusive, harassing, or otherwise unacceptable behavior may be reported to the community leaders responsible for enforcement privately through GitHub: open the repository's **Security** tab and choose **Report a vulnerability**, which reaches only the maintainers. Please say that the report concerns the Code of Conduct. All complaints will be reviewed and investigated promptly and fairly.

All community leaders are obligated to respect the privacy and security of the reporter of any incident.

## Enforcement Guidelines

Community leaders will follow these Community Impact Guidelines in determining the consequences for any action they deem in violation of this Code of Conduct:

### 1. Correction

**Community Impact**: Use of inappropriate language or other behavior deemed unprofessional or unwelcome in the community.

**Consequence**: A private, written warning from community leaders, providing clarity around the nature of the violation and an explanation of why the behavior was inappropriate. A public apology may be requested.

### 2. Warning

**Community Impact**: A violation through a single incident or series of actions.

**Consequence**: A warning with consequences for continued behavior. No interaction with the people involved, including unsolicited interaction with those enforcing the Code of Conduct, for a specified period of time. This includes avoiding interactions in community spaces as well as external channels like social media. Violating these terms may lead to a temporary or permanent ban.

### 3. Temporary Ban

**Community Impact**: A serious violation of community standards, including sustained inappropriate behavior.

**Consequence**: A temporary ban from any sort of interaction or public communication with the community for a specified period of time. No public or private interaction with the people involved, including unsolicited interaction with those enforcing the Code of Conduct, is allowed during this period. Violating these terms may lead to a permanent ban.

### 4. Permanent Ban

**Community Impact**: Demonstrating a pattern of violation of community standards, including sustained inappropriate behavior, harassment of an individual, or aggression toward or disparagement of classes of individuals.

**Consequence**: A permanent ban from any sort of public interaction within the community.

`CONTRIBUTING.md`:

```md
# Contributing to ClassRevive

Thanks for your interest. Bug reports, detection reports, documentation fixes, regression cases and code are all welcome. By taking part you agree to follow the [Code of Conduct](CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md).

## Ground rules

- **Never execute the analyzed code.** ClassRevive reads target files as data: it must never load, link or run a target class on a JVM, run its static initializers or start a target program. The few passes that evaluate target bytecode do it in a bounded static interpreter with an instruction allowlist (see [ARCHITECTURE.md](ARCHITECTURE.md#principles)). A change that breaks this rule will not be merged, whatever it gains.
- **Only analyze what you have the right to analyze**, and never share files you may not share. This applies to issues, pull requests, test fixtures and benchmark cases alike.
- **Fail closed and report evidence.** Refuse unsafe input with a diagnostic instead of guessing. Recompiling is not behavioral equivalence: do not describe a result as equivalent or "100% recovered" because it compiles.

## Reporting a bug

Open an issue with the **Bug report** form. The most useful report is one anyone can reproduce:

1. **A minimal case you wrote.** A few lines of Java (or Kotlin, Scala…) plus the exact compiler command and flags, for example `javac --release 17 -d out Example.java && jar cf example.jar -C out .`.
2. **Or a public library jar**, named by its Maven coordinates (`group:artifact:version`), never re-uploaded.
3. The ClassRevive command you ran, `classrevive --version`, `classrevive engines`, `java -version` and your operating system.
4. The relevant part of `report.txt` or `report.json`, with local paths, user names and strings from the input removed.

**Do not attach private, proprietary or third-party binaries** (jars, APKs, executables, class files), secrets or source you are not allowed to share, and do not post links to them. If you can only reproduce a problem with such a file, describe what the file looks like (compiler, obfuscator and settings, the construct that fails) and we will try to build an equivalent case.

Obfuscation detection mistakes (a tool reported that was not used, or missed) have their own form: paste the diagnosis output instead of the file. Security vulnerabilities go to the [security policy](SECURITY.md), never to a public issue.

## Building and testing

You need **JDK 21** (the build and the recompilation step use its `javac`) and the checked-in Gradle wrapper; nothing else has to be installed. From the repository root:

```bash
./gradlew test :cli:installDist :cli:distZip
```

On Windows, use `gradlew.bat` (or `.\gradlew` in PowerShell). This runs every unit and integration test, the committed regression cases in `benchmarks/regressions/`, and builds the distribution:

- `modules/cli/build/install/classrevive/bin/classrevive` (and `classrevive-gui`) — the launchers you can run directly;
- `modules/cli/build/distributions/classrevive-<version>.zip` — the distributable zip.

The desktop tests detect a headless environment and skip what needs a display. `ScreenshotTour` is opt-in and does not run by default.

Every downloaded dependency is checked against `gradle/verification-metadata.xml`. If you add or update a dependency, regenerate the metadata with `./gradlew --write-verification-metadata sha256 help`, review the diff, and update [THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md](THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md) and `third-party-licenses/` for anything that ships in the distribution. New dependencies need a license and transitive-dependency review; strong copyleft licenses (such as GPL or AGPL) cannot be bundled.

## Project layout

The build has 17 Gradle modules under `modules/`, from the immutable `model` up to the `gui` and `cli` front ends. [ARCHITECTURE.md](ARCHITECTURE.md) describes each module, the worker JVMs, the decompile flow, selection and the transforms; read it before a non-trivial change. Report fields are documented in [docs/reports.md](docs/reports.md) and obfuscation detection in [docs/obfuscation-detection.md](docs/obfuscation-detection.md).

## Making a change

1. For anything larger than a small fix, open an issue (or a discussion) first, so the approach can be agreed before you write the code.
2. Fork the repository and create a branch from `main` with a short descriptive name, such as `fix/jadx-placeholder-cast` or `docs/report-fields`.
3. Keep the change focused: one topic per pull request.
4. **Write the test first.** A bug fix comes with a test that fails without it; a new feature comes with tests of its behavior and its limits.
5. Run `./gradlew test :cli:installDist :cli:distZip` before you push.
6. Open the pull request against `main` and fill in the template. CI runs the same command on Linux, Windows and macOS. Pull requests are squash-merged.

### Commits

- Write commit messages in English, with a short imperative subject (`Fold constant string switches in the Procyon output`) of about 70 characters or fewer, and a body that explains *why* when it is not obvious.
- Do not reference private files, samples or internal notes in messages.
- Signing off your commits ([Developer Certificate of Origin](https://developercertificate.org/), `git commit -s`) is welcome but not required. Contributions are accepted under the project's license, the [ClassRevive License](LICENSE) (section 5).

### Code style

- Code, comments, documentation and commit messages are in English.
- Follow the style of the surrounding code; there is no separate formatter configuration.
- Keep diagnostic codes and report schemas stable. A change to `report.json` must be backward compatible or bump its schema version.
- Every new limit (time, size, count, steps) is explicit, and hitting it is reported.
- Anything that runs third-party or heavy code on data derived from the input runs in a worker JVM through `ProcessRunner`, never in the main process.

## Adding a test fixture or regression case

- Prefer fixtures the test generates itself: Java source compiled by the test, or classes written with ASM. Existing tests in each module show both patterns.
- Committed binaries must be written for this repository or derived from inputs under a license compatible with the ClassRevive License (permissive licenses such as MIT, BSD or Apache-2.0), and documented next to the file.
- Reduced classes from a third-party jar are still derived from it: do not commit them unless the original license allows it.
- To turn a decompilation failure into a permanent regression case, use the failure lab (`classrevive lab`, `lab-minimize`, `lab-promote`) as described in [benchmarks/regressions/README.md](benchmarks/regressions/README.md), and record the provenance and license.

## Adding a bytecode pass

Passes implement `BytecodePass` and are registered explicitly in `BuiltinPasses` (module `transforms`); there is no plugin discovery. The contract (bounded input and changes, an audit record for every modification, no target execution, behavior preserved or input left unchanged) is in [docs/pass-sdk.md](docs/pass-sdk.md). A new pass needs tests for the shapes it folds, for the shapes it must leave alone, and for its budgets, and its output must pass the JVM verifier.

## Engines and benchmarks

For a change to an engine adapter, selection or verification, measure it:

```bash
./gradlew benchmarkFixtures :cli:installDist
modules/cli/build/install/classrevive/bin/classrevive benchmark build/benchmark-corpus --output build/your-result --engines all
python scripts/check_benchmark.py build/your-result
```

Include the Markdown summary and the failing cases in the pull request. `./gradlew :cli:scoreboard` measures real libraries from Maven Central; rules must not be tuned on the `holdout` sets. Never lower a threshold to make a benchmark look better, and report results with the corpus, versions, resource budget and failures.

A new engine must run in its own worker JVM, must not discover user plugins, execute target code or inherit injected JVM flags, and its whole runtime dependency graph needs a license review.

## Translations

English is the reference language for the code, the documentation and the desktop application. Portuguese (Brazil) is maintained alongside it: the desktop strings in `modules/gui/src/main/resources/dev/classrevive/gui/messages_pt_BR.properties`, the beginner's guide `docs/guia-iniciante.md` and the Portuguese README.

- A new desktop string goes into both `messages.properties` and `messages_pt_BR.properties`; a test fails when the keys differ.
- If you cannot write Portuguese, add the English text to both files and say so in the pull request, so it can be translated before release.
- Other languages are not maintained for now. Open a discussion before starting one, with a plan for keeping it up to date.

## Coding agents

Automated and AI-assisted contributions follow the same rules; [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md) summarizes them. The contributor who opens the pull request is responsible for its content.

## Good first issues

Issues labeled `good first issue` are small, self-contained and come with a pointer to the code and the test to change. Comment on the issue before starting, so two people do not work on the same one.

```

`DISCLAIMER.md`:

```md
# Disclaimer

ClassRevive is a decompiler and deobfuscation tool. It turns compiled Java back into readable source and can undo some obfuscation. Tools like this have legitimate uses, and they can also be misused. This page explains what ClassRevive expects of you and what it does not promise.

## Analyze only what you have the right to analyze

Use ClassRevive on software you are entitled to examine. Typical cases:

- your own code, or code your organization owns and has asked you to work on;
- open-source software, under the terms of its license;
- software whose license, contract or written permission from the rights holder allows reverse engineering;
- cases where the law where you live allows it.

Do not use ClassRevive to infringe copyright, break license terms you agreed to, remove license checks or copy protection, take trade secrets, cheat in online services, or build software meant to harm people or systems.

## Reverse engineering and the law

Many legal systems allow some reverse engineering, for example to achieve interoperability between programs, to research or fix security problems, or to study how a program works. What is allowed, under which conditions, and how far a license agreement (EULA) can restrict it differ from country to country and change over time.

You are responsible for knowing and following the law that applies to you and the license terms of the software you analyze. **Nothing in this project is legal advice.** If you are unsure whether an analysis is allowed, ask a qualified lawyer before you start.

## Recovered code may belong to someone else

Decompiled source is derived from the original program. Its copyright and license stay with the original authors: decompiling a program does not give you any right to publish, redistribute or reuse its code. Results also contain code produced by third-party decompilers and may include material from libraries bundled in the input. Treat the output with the same care as the input.

## Trademarks and detection

Names of obfuscators, decompilers and other products mentioned in ClassRevive's code, reports and documentation, such as Zelix KlassMaster (ZKM), Allatori, DashO, Stringer, ProGuard, R8, Skidfuscator and Aidsfuscator, are trademarks or names of their respective owners. They are used only to identify the tools whose output ClassRevive recognizes. ClassRevive is not affiliated with, endorsed by or sponsored by any of them.

Obfuscator detection is heuristic. A report that names an obfuscator is a hypothesis with a score and the reasons behind it, not proof that the tool was used, and "unknown" or "none" are ordinary answers. Detection results say nothing about whether a program is safe, malicious, licensed or pirated.

## Handling suspicious files

ClassRevive never loads, links or runs the classes it analyzes, but parsers and decompilers can still have bugs. Analyze files you do not trust inside a disposable virtual machine. [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md) describes the exact boundary.

## No warranty

ClassRevive is provided "as is", without warranties or conditions of any kind, as stated in the [ClassRevive License](LICENSE). Recovered source may be incomplete, may not compile, and may behave differently from the original even when it compiles. You use the tool and its output at your own risk.

`README.md`:

```md
# ClassRevive

**Recover readable Java from compiled code, and measure how much of it is right.**

English | [Português (Brasil)](README.pt-BR.md)

![The ClassRevive desktop application showing a decompiled Gson class: package tree on the left, the selected source with a green round-trip dot next to each method in the middle, and the class's confidence level and evidence on the right](docs/images/desktop-class-dark.png)

ClassRevive runs four well-known Java decompilers (CFR, Vineflower, Procyon and JADX) on a `.class`, `.jar`, Android APK or an executable with an embedded jar. It recompiles every result with javac, compares it with the original bytecode, and keeps, file by file and method by method, the version the evidence supports. Every class ends up with a confidence level you can check, in a desktop application or on the command line.

## What it does

- **Decompiles with four engines and picks per file and per method.** Each engine runs in its own JVM. Candidates are ranked by whether they recompile, how many structural signatures match the original, and how many method bodies come back identical or equivalent after recompilation.
- **Verifies instead of guessing.** Every result says what was measured: recompilation, signatures per class, a round trip per method. Partial results keep a readable bytecode listing of what could not be recovered.
- **Handles awkward inputs.** Multi-release jars, class names that collide by letter case, executables that carry a jar, bundles of jars, Android APK and dex files (converted with dex2jar).
- **Detects obfuscation and undoes some of it.** A static profile names the techniques and the obfuscator they point to, with a score and the reasons. Two community obfuscators (Skidfuscator and Aidsfuscator) are reversed automatically, and Zelix KlassMaster opaque-predicate flags that are provably constant are folded.
- **Never runs the code it analyzes.** Target classes are never initialized and their methods are never invoked. See [Security](#security-and-responsible-use) for the precise boundary.

## What it does not do

- It does not prove that the recovered program behaves like the original. Behavior is always reported as `NOT_VERIFIED`.
- It cannot bring back what compilation threw away: comments, formatting and often local variable names.
- It does not recover names an obfuscator renamed, unless you supply the obfuscator's mapping file.
- Recompilation runs on JDK 21, so class files built for Java 22 or newer are read and listed but not verified.
- It is not a malware scanner or a sandbox. Its worker JVMs isolate faults, not hostile code.
- It does not decompile native code to Java. Bundled native libraries can be triaged, optionally with a Ghidra you install yourself.

## Quick start

**Requirement:** a Java 21 **JDK** (not only a JRE), because ClassRevive uses javac to check its results. [Eclipse Temurin 21](https://adoptium.net) works on Windows, Linux and macOS. `java -version` should print 21.

1. Download the zip of the latest release from the [Releases page](https://github.com/t1zzo/classrevive/releases) and unzip it anywhere.
2. Open the desktop application:

   ```bash
   bin/classrevive-gui
   ```

   On Windows, double-click `bin\classrevive-gui.bat`. Open or drop a `.jar`, press **F5** to decompile, and read each class with its confidence level.
3. Or use the command line:

   ```bash
   bin/classrevive decompile app.jar --engines all
   ```

   This writes a new `app-classrevive/` folder: the selected sources in `selection/sources/`, a confidence map in `report.html`, an IDE project in `project/`, and every engine's raw output next to them. Existing folders are never overwritten.

`classrevive --help` lists every command and `classrevive help decompile` explains one. To build from source instead, run `./gradlew :cli:installDist` with JDK 21; the launchers land in `modules/cli/build/install/classrevive/bin/`.

New to decompiling? Read [Getting started](docs/getting-started.md), or the [guia para iniciantes](docs/guia-iniciante.md) in Portuguese.

## Features

| Area | What you get | Docs |
|---|---|---|
| Desktop application | Package and class explorer, bytecode before any decompile, live progress with cancel, per-class confidence and per-method round-trip marks, javac errors underlined, side-by-side engine comparison, find usages and call hierarchy, go to class, code search, export as an IDE project, dark and light themes, English and Portuguese | [Getting started](docs/getting-started.md#4-the-desktop-application) |
| Verified selection | Recompilation, structural signatures, per-method round trip, bounded hybrids, compiler-guided source repairs, per-method composition across engines | [Architecture](ARCHITECTURE.md#selection-and-composition) |
| Inputs | `.class`, `.jar`, multi-release jars, executables with an embedded jar, bundles of jars, Android APK and dex | [CLI reference](docs/cli-reference.md#executables-bundles-and-android-inputs) |
| Missing libraries | Pass your own jars with `--classpath`; otherwise inferred stand-ins let the result compile, and it is marked stub-backed | [CLI reference](docs/cli-reference.md#selection-evidence-and-limits) |
| Obfuscation | Static technique profile and obfuscator hypotheses with scores; Skidfuscator and Aidsfuscator reversal; opaque-predicate flag folding; opt-in constant and string-decoding passes | [Obfuscation detection](docs/obfuscation-detection.md) |
| Renaming | Readable aliases, explicit mapping files, or a ProGuard/R8 mapping to restore original names where that is safe | [CLI reference](docs/cli-reference.md#rename-experimental) |
| Diagnostics | Static reflection, class-loading, invokedynamic and crypto clues; compiler fingerprint; embedded library recognition; optional Ghidra triage of native libraries | [CLI reference](docs/cli-reference.md#diagnose) |
| Reports | `report.txt`, `report.json` (schema v1), a self-contained `report.html` confidence map, IDE project export | [Report format](docs/reports.md) |
| Measurement | Benchmark command, a scoreboard on hash-checked Maven Central libraries, and a failure lab that turns failures into regression tests | [Benchmarks](docs/benchmarks.md) |

## How it works

```text
input (.class / .jar / .apk / .exe)
  │  bounded intake: read as data, never extracted or executed
  ▼
normalize ── dex2jar for Android · portable names · base version of multi-release jars
  │
  ▼
diagnose ── obfuscation profile; reverse a recognized obfuscator (checked by the JVM verifier)
  │
  ▼
CFR · Vineflower · Procyon · JADX        each in its own worker JVM
  │
  ▼
javac in a worker ── signatures per class · round trip per method
  │
  ▼
selection ── rank · hybrids · source repairs · per-method composition
  │
  ▼
selected sources + report.html / report.json + IDE project (+ bytecode fallback)
```

The details, including what each step refuses to do, are in [ARCHITECTURE.md](ARCHITECTURE.md).

## Benchmarks

The scoreboard decompiles real open-source libraries downloaded from Maven Central and checked by SHA-256. No rule in ClassRevive was tuned on the two holdout sets. Measured on 2026-10-29 with ClassRevive 0.1.0-dev, all four engines plus combined selection, on Windows with JDK 21:

| Set | Libraries | Compile as a whole | Signatures | Bodies, whole library | Bodies, with per-file credit |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `holdout` | 3 | 3/3 | 2,372/2,375 (99.8%) | 1,752/1,765 (99.2%) | 1,752/1,765 (99.2%) |
| `holdout2` | 13 | 5/13 | 21,583/52,080 (41.4%) | 8,774/38,445 (22.8%) | 35,899/38,445 (93.3%) |

- **Compile as a whole**: the selected sources of the whole library compile with javac against its declared dependencies. On `holdout2`, 8 of 13 libraries are still left with 1 to 33 javac errors.
- **Signatures**: classes, fields and methods whose structure matches the original, counted on the classes javac emitted; a library that does not compile contributes little here.
- **Bodies, whole library**: method bodies identical or equivalent to the original after recompilation, counted only for libraries that compile as a whole. The denominator is every method body of the original.
- **Bodies, with per-file credit**: the same, but each file of a library that does not compile is also compiled on its own against the original classes, and its bodies count when that file compiles. It measures how much of the code is right file by file, not a program you can rebuild.

None of these numbers measures behavior, and they say nothing certain about other inputs, especially obfuscated ones.

Reproduce them with a JDK 21 checkout:

```bash
./gradlew :cli:scoreboard -PscoreboardSet=holdout
./gradlew :cli:scoreboard -PscoreboardSet=holdout2
```

Each run writes `build/scoreboard/<set>-<timestamp>/benchmark.md`. Per-library numbers, the `dev` set and how to read every column are in [docs/benchmarks.md](docs/benchmarks.md).

## Security and responsible use

ClassRevive never runs the code it analyzes: no target class is initialized and no target method is invoked. Bytecode is read as data, and some passes evaluate pure constant code in a bounded static interpreter. After bytecode is rewritten (for example by an obfuscator reversal), the rewritten classes are linked, never initialized, in a separate worker JVM so that the JVM verifier can check them. Decompilers, javac and the other heavy steps run in separate worker JVMs with time, memory and output limits. That is fault isolation, **not an operating-system sandbox**: analyze deliberately hostile files inside a virtual machine.

Only analyze software you have the right to analyze: your own code, open-source code, or cases your license or the law allows. Read the [disclaimer](DISCLAIMER.md) before using ClassRevive on third-party software, and see [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md) to report a vulnerability. Please do not attach private or proprietary binaries to public issues.

Obfuscator and product names (Zelix KlassMaster, Allatori, DashO, Stringer, ProGuard, R8, Skidfuscator, Aidsfuscator and others) belong to their owners. ClassRevive is not affiliated with any of them, and its detection is heuristic.

`README.pt-BR.md`:

```md
# ClassRevive

**Recupere Java legível a partir de código compilado e meça o quanto dele está certo.**

[English](README.md) | Português (Brasil)

![O aplicativo desktop do ClassRevive mostrando uma classe descompilada do Gson: a árvore de pacotes à esquerda, o código escolhido com uma bolinha verde de ida e volta ao lado de cada método no meio, e o nível de confiança e as evidências da classe à direita](docs/images/desktop-class-dark-pt-BR.png)

O ClassRevive roda quatro descompiladores Java conhecidos (CFR, Vineflower, Procyon e JADX) sobre um `.class`, um `.jar`, um APK do Android ou um executável com um jar dentro. Ele recompila cada resultado com o javac, compara com o bytecode original e fica, arquivo por arquivo e método por método, com a versão que as evidências sustentam. Cada classe termina com um nível de confiança que você pode conferir, no aplicativo desktop ou na linha de comando.

> A documentação de referência é em inglês; este README e o [guia para iniciantes](docs/guia-iniciante.md) são traduzidos. Se houver diferença, vale a versão em inglês.

## O que ele faz

- **Descompila com quatro descompiladores e escolhe por arquivo e por método.** Cada descompilador roda na sua própria JVM. Os candidatos são ordenados por recompilar ou não, por quantas assinaturas estruturais batem com o original e por quantos corpos de método voltam idênticos ou equivalentes depois de recompilados.
- **Confere em vez de adivinhar.** Todo resultado diz o que foi medido: recompilação, assinaturas por classe, ida e volta por método. Resultados parciais guardam uma listagem legível do bytecode do que não pôde ser recuperado.
- **Lida com entradas difíceis.** Jars multi-release, nomes de classe que colidem por maiúsculas e minúsculas, executáveis que carregam um jar, pacotes de jars, APK e dex do Android (convertidos com o dex2jar).
- **Detecta ofuscação e desfaz parte dela.** Um perfil estático aponta as técnicas e o ofuscador que elas indicam, com uma pontuação e os motivos. Dois ofuscadores comunitários (Skidfuscator e Aidsfuscator) são revertidos automaticamente, e as flags de predicado opaco do Zelix KlassMaster comprovadamente constantes são simplificadas.
- **Nunca executa o código que analisa.** As classes analisadas nunca são inicializadas e os métodos delas nunca são chamados. Veja [Segurança](#segurança-e-uso-responsável) para a fronteira exata.

## O que ele não faz

- Não prova que o programa recuperado se comporta como o original. O comportamento é sempre informado como `NOT_VERIFIED`.
- Não traz de volta o que a compilação descartou: comentários, formatação e, muitas vezes, os nomes das variáveis locais.
- Não recupera nomes que um ofuscador trocou, a menos que você forneça o arquivo de mapeamento do ofuscador.
- A recompilação roda no JDK 21; por isso, arquivos `.class` feitos para Java 22 ou mais novo são lidos e listados, mas não conferidos.
- Não é antivírus nem sandbox. As JVMs auxiliares isolam falhas, não código hostil.
- Não descompila código nativo para Java. Bibliotecas nativas incluídas podem passar por triagem, opcionalmente com um Ghidra que você mesmo instala.

## Começo rápido

**Requisito:** um **JDK** do Java 21 (não só o JRE), porque o ClassRevive usa o javac para conferir os resultados. O [Eclipse Temurin 21](https://adoptium.net) funciona no Windows, no Linux e no macOS. `java -version` deve mostrar 21.

1. Baixe o zip da versão mais recente na [página de Releases](https://github.com/t1zzo/classrevive/releases) e descompacte onde quiser.
2. Abra o aplicativo desktop:

   ```bash
   bin/classrevive-gui
   ```

   No Windows, dê dois cliques em `bin\classrevive-gui.bat`. Abra ou arraste um `.jar`, aperte **F5** para descompilar e leia cada classe com o seu nível de confiança.
3. Ou use a linha de comando:

   ```bash
   bin/classrevive decompile app.jar --engines all
   ```

   Isso cria uma pasta nova `app-classrevive/`: o código escolhido em `selection/sources/`, um mapa de confiança em `report.html`, um projeto de IDE em `project/` e, ao lado, a saída bruta de cada descompilador. Pastas existentes nunca são sobrescritas.

`classrevive --help` lista todos os comandos e `classrevive help decompile` explica um deles. Para montar a partir do código-fonte, rode `./gradlew :cli:installDist` com o JDK 21; os atalhos ficam em `modules/cli/build/install/classrevive/bin/`.

Nunca descompilou nada? Leia o [guia para iniciantes](docs/guia-iniciante.md).

## Como funciona

```text
entrada (.class / .jar / .apk / .exe)
  │  leitura limitada: tratada como dados, nunca extraída nem executada
  ▼
normalização ── dex2jar para Android · nomes portáveis · versão base de jars multi-release
  │
  ▼
diagnóstico ── perfil de ofuscação; reverte um ofuscador reconhecido (conferido pelo verificador da JVM)
  │
  ▼
CFR · Vineflower · Procyon · JADX        cada um na sua própria JVM auxiliar
  │
  ▼
javac numa JVM auxiliar ── assinaturas por classe · ida e volta por método
  │
  ▼
seleção ── ordenação · híbridos · reparos de código · composição por método
  │
  ▼
código escolhido + report.html / report.json + projeto de IDE (+ bytecode de reserva)
```

Os detalhes, incluindo o que cada etapa se recusa a fazer, estão no [ARCHITECTURE.md](ARCHITECTURE.md) (em inglês).

## Benchmarks

O placar descompila bibliotecas reais de código aberto baixadas do Maven Central e conferidas por SHA-256. Nenhuma regra do ClassRevive foi ajustada nos dois conjuntos de validação (*holdout*). Medido em 29/10/2026 com o ClassRevive 0.1.0-dev, com os quatro descompiladores e a seleção combinada, no Windows com o JDK 21:

| Conjunto | Bibliotecas | Compilam inteiras | Assinaturas | Corpos, biblioteca inteira | Corpos, com crédito por arquivo |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `holdout` | 3 | 3/3 | 2.372/2.375 (99,8%) | 1.752/1.765 (99,2%) | 1.752/1.765 (99,2%) |
| `holdout2` | 13 | 5/13 | 21.583/52.080 (41,4%) | 8.774/38.445 (22,8%) | 35.899/38.445 (93,3%) |

- **Compilam inteiras**: o código escolhido da biblioteca inteira compila com o javac contra as dependências que ela declara. No `holdout2`, 8 das 13 bibliotecas ainda ficam com 1 a 33 erros do javac.
- **Assinaturas**: classes, campos e métodos cuja estrutura bate com o original, contados nas classes que o javac gerou; uma biblioteca que não compila contribui pouco aqui.
- **Corpos, biblioteca inteira**: corpos de método idênticos ou equivalentes ao original depois de recompilados, contados só nas bibliotecas que compilam inteiras. O denominador é todo corpo de método do original.
- **Corpos, com crédito por arquivo**: o mesmo, mas cada arquivo de uma biblioteca que não compila também é compilado sozinho contra as classes originais, e os corpos dele contam quando esse arquivo compila. Isso mede quanto do código está certo arquivo por arquivo, não um programa que dá para recompilar.

Nenhum desses números mede comportamento, e eles não garantem nada sobre outras entradas, principalmente as ofuscadas.

Para reproduzir, numa cópia do repositório com o JDK 21:

```bash
./gradlew :cli:scoreboard -PscoreboardSet=holdout
./gradlew :cli:scoreboard -PscoreboardSet=holdout2
```

Cada execução grava `build/scoreboard/<conjunto>-<data-hora>/benchmark.md`. Os números por biblioteca, o conjunto `dev` e como ler cada coluna estão em [docs/benchmarks.md](docs/benchmarks.md) (em inglês).

## Segurança e uso responsável

O ClassRevive nunca executa o código que analisa: nenhuma classe analisada é inicializada e nenhum método dela é chamado. O bytecode é lido como dados, e alguns passes avaliam código constante puro num interpretador estático com limites. Depois que o bytecode é reescrito (por exemplo, pela reversão de um ofuscador), as classes reescritas são linkadas, nunca inicializadas, numa JVM auxiliar separada, para que o verificador da JVM as confira. Descompiladores, javac e as outras etapas pesadas rodam em JVMs auxiliares separadas, com limites de tempo, memória e saída. Isso é isolamento de falhas, **não uma sandbox do sistema operacional**: analise arquivos deliberadamente hostis dentro de uma máquina virtual.

Só analise software que você tem o direito de analisar: seu próprio código, código aberto, ou casos que a sua licença ou a lei permitem. Leia o [aviso legal](DISCLAIMER.md) (em inglês) antes de usar o ClassRevive em software de terceiros, e veja o [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md) (em inglês) para relatar uma vulnerabilidade. Por favor, não anexe binários privados ou proprietários em issues públicas.

Os nomes de ofuscadores e produtos (Zelix KlassMaster, Allatori, DashO, Stringer, ProGuard, R8, Skidfuscator, Aidsfuscator e outros) pertencem aos seus donos. O ClassRevive não tem vínculo com nenhum deles, e a detecção é heurística.

`SECURITY.md`:

```md
# Security policy

ClassRevive reads untrusted bytecode by design. This page explains which versions get security fixes, how to report a vulnerability, and where the security boundary is.

## Supported versions

ClassRevive is pre-1.0. Security fixes go into the latest release only.

| Version | Supported |
|---|---|
| Latest 0.x release | Yes |
| Older releases | No; please upgrade |
| Unreleased development builds | Best effort |

## Reporting a vulnerability

Please report vulnerabilities privately, not in public issues, discussions or pull requests.

1. Open the repository's **Security** tab and choose **Report a vulnerability**. This uses GitHub's private vulnerability reporting: only you and the maintainers can see the report.
2. Describe the problem, the affected version, and how to reproduce it. A minimal input you built yourself is the most useful reproducer. Do not attach private or proprietary binaries, credentials or live malware; if a reproducer needs a third-party file, describe how to obtain it instead.
3. If the **Report a vulnerability** button is not available, open a public issue that only asks for a private channel, with no technical details, and wait for a maintainer to reply.

ClassRevive is maintained by volunteers, so please be patient. Give the maintainers a reasonable time to release a fix before you disclose the problem publicly, and say whether you would like to be credited in the release notes.

Useful reports include: a crafted input that makes ClassRevive execute target code, write outside its output folder, overwrite an existing file, escape its resource limits in a way that harms the host, or inject terminal escape sequences into its output. Decompilation that is merely wrong, incomplete or slow is a normal bug: open a regular issue.

## Security boundary

**ClassRevive never runs the code it analyzes.** Target bytecode is read as data with ASM. No target class is ever initialized, no target method or constructor is ever invoked, and the target program is never started. Some passes evaluate pure constant code in a bounded static interpreter: string and number decoders of known obfuscators and integer folds, with an explicit instruction allowlist and step and memory budgets. That interpreter does not define classes or call target methods.

One step does load target-derived classes into a JVM, only to verify them. After bytecode is rewritten (an obfuscator reversal, a whole-jar `transform` pass, or a failure-lab reduction), a separate worker JVM defines the classes in an isolated class loader and links them, so the JVM bytecode verifier checks them. The classes are never initialized and none of their code runs there.

What the rest of the pipeline does:

- **Intake** reads archives in the main process under fixed limits: 256 MiB input, 16 MiB per expanded entry, 512 MiB expanded in total and 20,000 entries. Entries are never extracted to disk or executed. Unsafe archive names, duplicate paths and identity mismatches are reported or refused.
- **Decompilers, javac, dex2jar, the transform and rename passes, the bytecode fallback and the link check** each run in a separate JVM with a wall-clock timeout, heap and metaspace limits, a retained-log limit and an output budget. `JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS`, `_JAVA_OPTIONS`, `JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS` and `CLASSPATH` are removed from their environment.
- **javac** runs with annotation processing disabled (`-proc:none`), `-implicit:none`, an always-empty source path and either an empty class path or the dependency jars you pass explicitly. It never loads the classes it compiles. No Gradle or Maven build from the input is ever run, and dependencies are never downloaded.
- **JADX** uses a fixed list of input plugins, with its cache, configuration and temporary files kept under the worker's output folder. External plugin discovery and scripting are not enabled.
- **Native libraries** found with `--native` are extracted as data into the output folder and only read, by ClassRevive and by a Ghidra installation you provide. They are never loaded or run.
- **Output folders** must not exist yet. Nothing is overwritten.

### What this boundary does not cover

- Worker JVMs provide **fault isolation, not an operating-system sandbox**. They inherit the rest of the user's environment and can read and write the file system with the user's permissions. A bug in a decompiler, in javac, in the JVM verifier or in ClassRevive's own parsers could be exploitable by a crafted input.
- The JDK parses a zip's central directory before ClassRevive counts its entries, and the initial intake has byte limits but no wall-clock deadline.
- Input hashes are taken before and after reading. They detect ordinary concurrent changes; they are not an atomic snapshot. Use immutable copies of adversarial inputs and do not modify the output tree while a job runs.
- Disk budgets are sampled while a worker runs, so a short overshoot is possible.
- Obfuscator detection and the static diagnostics are triage clues. They are not a malware scan and do not prove that a file is safe.

**Analyze deliberately hostile or untrusted files inside a disposable virtual machine** with no access to your personal files or credentials, and treat everything ClassRevive writes as derived from that input.

### Future behavioral verification

Behavioral comparison is not implemented and target execution is disabled. If it is added, it must run only inside an isolated sandbox and fail closed when that sandbox is unavailable. It must never fall back to running target code on the host.

## Responsible use

Analyze only software you have the right to analyze. See [DISCLAIMER.md](DISCLAIMER.md).

```

| dex2jar (de.femtopedia.dex2jar: dex-translator, dex-reader, dex-reader-api, dex-ir, d2j-base-cmd, d2j-external), Copyright Panxiaobo and contributors, https://github.com/ThexXTURBOXx/dex2jar | 2.4.38 | Apache-2.0 | `third-party-licenses/dex2jar-Apache-2.0.txt`, `third-party-licenses/dex2jar-NOTICE.txt` |
| Android Open Source Project `dx`, repackaged unmodified inside `d2j-external` | as shipped in dex2jar 2.4.38 | Apache-2.0, Copyright The Android Open Source Project | `third-party-licenses/AOSP-dx-NOTICE.txt` |
| ASM tree, util, analysis and commons (requested by dex2jar) | 9.10.1 | BSD-3-Clause | `third-party-licenses/ASM-BSD-3-Clause.txt` |

`d2j-external` also repackages ASM's core classes (BSD-3-Clause); the worker uses that ASM core, which is why these jars stay off the application's class path. This build also runs `dx` from that jar as a build tool, only to regenerate the test fixture in `benchmarks/android`.

## Optional external tool (not redistributed)

Ghidra (https://github.com/NationalSecurityAgency/ghidra), Apache-2.0. ClassRevive neither bundles nor downloads it; `--native` uses an installation the user already has (`--ghidra-home` or `GHIDRA_INSTALL_DIR`) and runs its `support/analyzeHeadless` launcher as a separate process. The post script `modules/pipeline/src/main/resources/dev/classrevive/pipeline/ghidra/ClassReviveNativeExport.java` is original ClassRevive code written against Ghidra's public scripting API; it is compiled by the user's Ghidra at run time, not by this build.

## Obfuscators ClassRevive interoperates with

ClassRevive recognizes and reverses the output of some obfuscators. This is interoperability by reading behaviour: the detectors and reversal passes were written from the bytecode these tools emit and from reading what their output does. No code of these tools is copied into ClassRevive, and none of them is bundled or run by the distribution.

- **Skidfuscator** (https://github.com/skidfuscatordev/skidfuscator-java-obfuscator), MIT, Copyright (c) 2021 Shanyu Juneja, full license `third-party-licenses/Skidfuscator-MIT.txt`. Benchmark fixture only (not part of the CLI distribution): `benchmarks/obfuscated/skidfuscator/skid-fixture-obf.jar` is ClassRevive's own fixture source obfuscated by Skidfuscator 2.1.0 (commit `e4c0f981911703e86ac8a2b1a77d7cfd18b9d719`). The jar carries the code Skidfuscator injects (decryptors, hash factory) and its `sdk/*` runtime, a copy of OpenHFT zero-allocation-hashing (XXH3), Apache-2.0. Skidfuscator runs only as an external tool when the corpus is regenerated.
- **Aidsfuscator** 2.10.0 (no license published upstream). Nothing of it is committed or distributed: `benchmarks/obfuscated/aidsfuscator/` holds only ClassRevive's own answer-key source, and obfuscated output is produced locally by whoever runs the corpus script.
- Commercial obfuscators named by the detector (Zelix KlassMaster, Allatori, Stringer, DashO, ProGuard/R8) are recognized from documented static patterns only (`docs/obfuscation-detection.md`). Their names are trademarks of their owners; ClassRevive is not affiliated with any of them.

## Build and test tooling (not in the distribution)

Gradle 8.12.1 (Apache-2.0); its wrapper is checked in and its distribution retains its own notices. Test-only: JUnit Jupiter/Platform (EPL-2.0), OpenTest4J and API Guardian (Apache-2.0). ProGuard 7.10.0 (GPL-2.0 with exception) was used only as an external tool to produce the committed ProGuard fixtures, which contain only ClassRevive's own classes. Test libraries are not included in the CLI distribution.

Gradle dependency verification metadata records SHA-256 values from the initial Maven Central resolution. This is trust-on-first-use integrity pinning, not independent signature authentication.

`benchmarks/android/src/demo/notes/Note.java`:

```java
package demo.notes;

import demo.util.Strings;

public final class Note {
    private final String title;
    private final String body;
    private final Priority priority;
    private int edits;

    public Note(String title, String body, Priority priority) {
        this.title = Strings.trimToEmpty(title);
        this.body = body == null ? "" : body;
        this.priority = priority;
    }

    public String title() { return title; }
    public String body() { return body; }
    public Priority priority() { return priority; }
    public int edits() { return edits; }

    public Note edit(String newBody) {
        Note next = new Note(title, newBody, priority);
        next.edits = edits + 1;
        return next;
    }

    public int words() {
        int count = 0;
        boolean inWord = false;
        for (int i = 0; i < body.length(); i++) {
            boolean letter = !Character.isWhitespace(body.charAt(i));
            if (letter && !inWord) count++;
            inWord = letter;
        }
        return count;
    }

    @Override public boolean equals(Object other) {
        if (this == other) return true;
        if (!(other instanceof Note)) return false;
        Note note = (Note) other;
        return title.equals(note.title) && body.equals(note.body) && priority == note.priority;
    }

    @Override public int hashCode() { return 31 * (31 * title.hashCode() + body.hashCode()) + priority.hashCode(); }

    @Override public String toString() { return "Note[" + title + ", " + priority + ", " + words() + " words]"; }
}

`benchmarks/android/src/demo/notes/NoteStore.java`:

```java
package demo.notes;

import android.util.Log;
import java.util.*;

public class NoteStore {
    private static final String TAG = "NoteStore";
    private final Map<String, Note> notes = new LinkedHashMap<String, Note>();

    public static final class Stats {
        public final int count;
        public final int words;
        Stats(int count, int words) { this.count = count; this.words = words; }
    }

    public synchronized void put(Note note) {
        if (note == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("note");
        notes.put(note.title(), note);
        Log.d(TAG, "stored " + note.title());
    }

    public synchronized Note get(String title) { return notes.get(title); }

    public List<Note> byPriority() {
        List<Note> sorted = new ArrayList<Note>(notes.values());
        Collections.sort(sorted, new Comparator<Note>() {
            @Override public int compare(Note a, Note b) {
                int byWeight = b.priority().weight() - a.priority().weight();
                return byWeight != 0 ? byWeight : a.title().compareTo(b.title());
            }
        });
        return sorted;
    }

    public Stats stats() {
        int words = 0;
        for (Note note : notes.values()) words += note.words();
        return new Stats(notes.size(), words);
    }

    public int load(String[] lines) {
        int loaded = 0;
        for (String line : lines) {
            String[] parts = line.split("\\|", 3);
            try {
                put(new Note(parts[0], parts.length > 2 ? parts[2] : "", Priority.parse(parts[1])));
                loaded++;
            } catch (ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException malformed) {
                Log.w(TAG, "skipped: " + line);
            }
        }
        return loaded;
    }
}

package demo.notes;

public enum Priority {
    LOW(1), NORMAL(2), HIGH(3);

    private final int weight;

    Priority(int weight) { this.weight = weight; }

    public int weight() { return weight; }

    public static Priority parse(String text) {
        switch (text.toLowerCase()) {
            case "low": return LOW;
            case "high": case "urgent": return HIGH;
            default: return NORMAL;
        }
    }
}

public final class Strings {

    public static String repeat(char c, int times) {
        if (times < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("times < 0");
        char[] out = new char[times];
        java.util.Arrays.fill(out, c);
        return new String(out);

`benchmarks/obfuscated/aidsfuscator/README.md`:

```md
# Aidsfuscator fixture (`fixtures.aids`)

The answer-key program for the Aidsfuscator reversal. `src/` is the program of the
Skidfuscator corpus (`../skidfuscator`) in package `fixtures.aids`, authored for ClassRevive.

Aidsfuscator's repository has no license, so neither the obfuscator nor anything it produced is committed here. The
obfuscated jar is made locally, under `.analysis/` (never committed):

1. Clone <https://github.com/LvStrnggg/aidsfuscator> at commit `8dbc9b09b760d38f5aa8cff619641cc4c9e4a3dc` (v2.10.0) and
   read it (it only reads the input jar and asks GitHub's API for its latest release).
2. Compile `aidsfuscator-api/src` and `aidsfuscator-main/src` with a JDK 25 (`javac -d classes`) against ASM 9.11.1
   (`asm`, `asm-tree`, `asm-commons`, `asm-util`, `asm-analysis`) and Gson 2.13.1.
3. Compile `src/` with `javac --release 8 -proc:none` into `in.jar` (main class `fixtures.aids.Main`).
4. Use the repository's `workspace/config.json`, `exclusions.json` and `references.json`, with `initOrder.json` set to
   `[]` and, in `config.json`, `trim`, `renameFields`, `renameMethods` and `renameClasses` disabled (renaming cannot be
   reversed without a mapping and would hide every name from `compare-reference`). Every other transformer stays on.
5. From the folder holding `in.jar` and `workspace/`:
   `java -cp <classes and libraries> dev.lvstrng.aidsfuscator.Main --config=config.json --exclusions=exclusions.json --initOrder=initOrder.json --references=references.json`
   writes `out.jar`.
6. `classrevive transform out.jar --output t --passes aidsfuscator`, then
   `classrevive decompile t/worker/transformed/transformed.jar --output d --engines all` and
   `classrevive compare-reference in.jar d --output r`.

Aidsfuscator draws its keys from `SecureRandom`, so every run gives different bytes; record the SHA-256 of
`in.jar` and `out.jar` with any measurement.

```

package fixtures.aids;

/** An enum with a constructor argument and a constant-specific body. */
public enum Kind {
    FOOD("food"),
    RENT("rent"),
    OTHER("other") {
        @Override
        public boolean essential() {
            return false;
        }
    };

    private final String code;

    Kind(String code) {
        this.code = code;
    }

    public String code() {
        return code;
    }

    public boolean essential() {
        return true;
    }

    public static Kind fromCode(String code) {
        for (Kind kind : values()) {
            if (kind.code.equals(code)) {
                return kind;
            }
        }
        return OTHER;
    }
}

`benchmarks/obfuscated/aidsfuscator/src/fixtures/aids/Ledger.java`:

```java
package fixtures.aids;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Collections;
import java.util.List;

/** Authored for ClassRevive's obfuscator corpora (Skidfuscator, Aidsfuscator): instance methods called from inside the jar, loops and exceptions. */
public class Ledger {
    private final List<Entry> entries = new ArrayList<>();
    private final String owner;
    private int version;

    public Ledger(String owner) {
        if (owner == null || owner.isEmpty()) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("owner required");
        }
        this.owner = owner;
    }

    public void add(String label, Kind kind, long cents) {
        if (cents < 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative amount: " + cents);
        }
        entries.add(new Entry(label, kind, cents));
        version++;
    }

    public long total(Kind kind) {
        long sum = 0;
        for (Entry entry : entries) {
            if (kind == null || entry.kind() == kind) {
                sum += entry.cents();
            }
        }
        return sum;
    }

    public int count() {
        return entries.size();
    }

    public List<String> labels() {
        List<String> labels = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < entries.size(); i++) {
            labels.add(i + ":" + entries.get(i).label());
        }
        Collections.sort(labels);
        return labels;
    }

    public String owner() {
        return owner;
    }

    public int version() {
        return version;
    }

    public long parseAndAdd(String label, String amount) {
        try {
            long cents = Long.parseLong(amount.trim());
            add(label, Kind.OTHER, cents);
            return cents;
        } catch (NumberFormatException e) {
            return -1;
        } finally {
            version += 10;
        }
    }

    public static final class Entry {
        private final String label;
        private final Kind kind;
        private final long cents;

        Entry(String label, Kind kind, long cents) {
            this.label = label;
            this.kind = kind;
            this.cents = cents;
        }

        public String label() { return label; }
        public Kind kind() { return kind; }
        public long cents() { return cents; }

        @Override
        public String toString() {
            return label + "=" + cents + " (" + kind + ")";
        }
    }
}

```

```java
package fixtures.aids;

import java.util.function.Function;

/** Entry point: lambdas, method references, nested try/catch and a static initializer. */
public class Main {
    static final String GREETING;
    private static int calls;

    static {
        GREETING = "ledger v" + 2;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Ledger ledger = new Ledger("ana");
        ledger.add("bread", Kind.FOOD, 350);
        ledger.add("flat", Kind.RENT, 120000);
        ledger.parseAndAdd("misc", " 42 ");
        ledger.parseAndAdd("bad", "x");
        try {
            ledger.add("broken", Kind.OTHER, -5);
        } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
            System.out.println("rejected: " + e.getMessage());
        }
        Function<Long, String> money = cents -> cents / 100 + "." + cents % 100;
        System.out.println(GREETING + " " + ledger.owner() + " " + money.apply(ledger.total(null)));
        ledger.labels().forEach(System.out::println);
        System.out.println(Shapes.describe(new Shapes.Rect(2, 3)) + " " + Shapes.weight(7) + " " + Shapes.command("pause"));
        System.out.println(count() + " " + Kind.fromCode("rent").essential());
    }

    static int count() {
        return ++calls;
    }
}
