.\modules\cli\build\install\classrevive\bin\classrevive.bat lab-promote build\lab-min\minimized --output benchmarks\regressions\my-case --provenance "authored fixture, Apache-2.0"
.\modules\cli\build\install\classrevive\bin\classrevive.bat lab-check benchmarks\regressions --output build\regression-check
```

`lab <input>` decompiles with every engine and writes one `failures/failure-NNNN/` case per failure: a method body that differs after recompilation, a candidate file javac rejects, an engine stub marker, or a worker failure. Cases are grouped in `failures.json`/`failures.md` by a stable signature such as `METHOD_DIFFERENT:cfr:body-differs:astore/dup` (category, producer, first diverging opcodes or javac code). Signatures never name target classes, members, constants or paths. The target-derived evidence (classes, candidate source, javac messages) stays in the case directory. With a corpus directory, `lab` runs the benchmark with the same capture. `lab-minimize` reduces a case with ASM (other classes, other members, stub bodies, instruction edits, debug attributes). A reduction is kept only if the real JVM verifier accepts every class, linked in an isolated loader without initializing or running anything, and two fresh runs reproduce the same signature. By default, an engine that recovered the method must keep recovering it. `--max-steps`, `--max-seconds` and `--timeout-seconds` bound the work. `lab-promote` measures the per-method level of every variant twice and writes `expected.json`. `lab-check`, `./gradlew test` and `./gradlew checkRegressions` fail when a committed case in `benchmarks/regressions/` gets worse. Commit only cases reduced from authored or license-compatible inputs.

JSON is UTF-8, object keys sorted, enums stable within schema v1. `behavior` is always `NOT_VERIFIED`. `report.json` is emitted when verified-job processing completes (including partial results); early intake failures still use `failure.txt` and benchmark failed rows. Per-worker limits are inherited, not a global benchmark disk/time budget; large corpora can consume substantial space in retained alternatives and compile attempts. See [report format](reports.md).

```

`docs/dynamic-diagnostics.md`:

```md
# Dynamic linkage diagnostics

```bat
classrevive diagnose target.jar --output diagnostic-result --timeout-seconds 60
```

Reads a .class or .jar snapshot and inventories it before scanning in a heap/time/output-limited worker. Does not extract classes, load the target, invoke bootstraps, resolve reflective targets or label software as malicious. The output directory must be new. Timeout defaults to 60 seconds, range 1..3600, for the worker; initial snapshot/inventory has byte limits but no wall-clock limit.

`diagnostics.json` contains snapshot SHA-256, worker outcome, scanned-class count, a sorted `signal_counts` map, and findings with archive entry, internal class, method/descriptor and instruction ordinal. Counts cover retained findings only; when status is `PARTIAL`, the counts may be incomplete. Ordinals count JVM instructions within a method, excluding labels/debug/frame metadata; they are not file byte offsets. Archive entry attribution distinguishes multi-release variants.

Categories:
- `INVOKEDYNAMIC`: bootstrap owner/name/descriptor and argument count. Standard lambda/string-concatenation sites also appear; their presence alone is not obfuscation.
- `CONSTANT_DYNAMIC`: bootstrap metadata, including nested dynamic constants to depth eight.
- `REFLECTION_API`: references to selected Class lookup methods, java.lang.reflect APIs and MethodHandles.Lookup APIs. This pattern list is intentionally incomplete and findings do not prove runtime reachability.
- `CLASS_LOADING_API`: selected `ClassLoader.loadClass`/`defineClass` calls, including calls owned by a class that directly extends `ClassLoader`, plus selected `MethodHandles.Lookup` class-definition calls. These can be used by plugin systems and ordinary frameworks.
- `CRYPTO_API`: selected JCE, `MessageDigest`, `KeyFactory` and `Signature` API calls. These references do not establish that class or string data is encrypted or decrypted.

The two additional categories are triage clues only. Their presence together does not identify a packer, prove encrypted payloads, establish that the methods run, or indicate malware. `diagnostics.json` includes this interpretation explicitly; no packer verdict is produced.

String literal contents and bootstrap argument values are omitted from reports. They remain in original artifacts; no redaction guarantee is made. Direct method-handle constants, native code, custom reflection wrappers and resolved runtime values are outside this version's coverage.

Budgets: 10,000 findings globally, 20,000 archive entries, 16 MiB per class, 512 MiB scanned class bytes; parent inventory limits also apply. Reaching the finding budget or nesting limit marks `PARTIAL` conservatively even if no further site is known. `SCANNED` means the documented patterns were scanned, not complete semantic understanding. CLI exit 0 means worker success without a coverage limit; exit 1 means partial/failure, exit 2 invalid syntax, 130 interruption. Worker failures retain their status/log and snapshot; intake failures are printed by the CLI and retain any already-created snapshot.

Serialized worker evidence is additionally capped at 16 MiB. Findings beyond that budget are omitted with explicit PARTIAL coverage; retained class count indicates scanning work, not that every finding from those classes fit in the report.

## Obfuscation profile

The same worker pass builds a static obfuscation profile: `diagnostics.json` gains `obfuscation` (techniques with class and occurrence counts and up to 10 samples, raw `indicators`, `verdict`, `hypotheses` with score, confidence and reasons, a one-line `summary`), and `obfuscation.txt` holds the readable form the CLI also prints. Resources contribute only their names and sizes (a bundled native library is never read). Rules, thresholds and limits are in [obfuscation detection](obfuscation-detection.md). The suggested obfuscator is a hypothesis, not proof.

```

`docs/getting-started.md`:

```md
# Getting started

This guide is for people who have never decompiled anything. It shows how to install ClassRevive, decompile a jar in the desktop application or on the command line, and understand the result. A Portuguese version is in [guia-iniciante.md](guia-iniciante.md).

## 1. What decompiling means

A Java program is usually shipped compiled: instead of the `.java` files the programmer wrote, you get `.class` files, often packed together in a `.jar`. Those files are meant for the Java virtual machine, not for people. **Decompiling** goes the other way, turning `.class` and `.jar` files back into readable `.java` code.

ClassRevive does not decompile on its own. It runs **four established decompilers** (CFR, Vineflower, Procyon and JADX), compares their results and keeps the best one, file by file and even method by method. Then it **checks** the result: it recompiles the generated code and compares it with the original bytecode.

| It does | It does not |
|---|---|
| Turn a `.jar`, `.class`, Android `.apk` or an `.exe` with an embedded jar into `.java` code | Bring back comments, formatting or most local variable names; compilation discarded them |
| Check whether the generated code compiles again | Prove that the program behaves like the original |
| Tell you how many methods came back identical or equivalent to the original | Run the program it analyzes; that is deliberate, for safety |
| Read class files of any Java version up to 28 | Recompile and verify class files built for Java 22 or newer |

> **Only decompile software you have the right to analyze**: your own code, open-source code, or cases your license or the law allows. See the [disclaimer](../DISCLAIMER.md).

## 2. What you need installed

Just one thing: a **Java 21 JDK**.

1. Download **Eclipse Temurin 21 (JDK)** from [adoptium.net](https://adoptium.net) for your system (on Windows, the `.msi` installer).
2. Install it with the default options. On Windows, if you see **Set JAVA_HOME variable**, enable it.
3. Check it: open a terminal (PowerShell on Windows, Terminal on macOS or Linux) and run:

   ```bash
   java -version
   ```

   The output should mention `21`, for example `openjdk version "21.0.12"`. If the command is not found, close and reopen the terminal; if it still fails, reinstall and enable the PATH/JAVA_HOME option.

> It has to be the **JDK**, not only a JRE: ClassRevive uses the Java compiler to check its results.

## 3. Get ClassRevive

Download the zip of the latest release from the [Releases page](https://github.com/t1zzo/classrevive/releases) and unzip it into a folder of your choice, for example `Documents\classrevive` on Windows or `~/classrevive` on macOS and Linux. Inside you will find:

| Folder | Contents |
|---|---|
| `bin/` | the launchers: `classrevive-gui` (desktop application) and `classrevive` (command line), with `.bat` versions for Windows |
| `lib/` | the program and the decompilers it runs |
| `docs/` | this documentation |
| `third-party-licenses/` | license texts of the bundled libraries |

To check that it works, open a terminal in that folder and run:

```bash
bin/classrevive engines
```

On Windows, write `bin\classrevive.bat engines`. It should list the four decompilers (`cfr`, `vineflower`, `procyon`, `jadx`) with their versions.

<details>
<summary>Building from source instead</summary>

With a JDK 21 and a checkout of the repository, run `./gradlew :cli:installDist` (`.\gradlew.bat :cli:installDist` on Windows). The first build downloads its dependencies and takes a few minutes. The launchers are then in `modules/cli/build/install/classrevive/bin/`. See the [command-line reference](cli-reference.md#build-from-source).

</details>

## 4. The desktop application

Start `bin/classrevive-gui` (on Windows, double-click `bin\classrevive-gui.bat`).

1. **Open a file.** Use **Open file…** or drop a `.jar`, `.class`, `.apk` or `.exe` on the window. The explorer on the left lists packages, classes and resources right away; you can read any class's bytecode before decompiling.
2. **Decompile.** Press **F5** (or the orange **Decompile** button). The activity panel at the bottom shows each step live, and the stop button cancels. **Decompile with options…** lets you pick the engines, the time limit and the libraries the program needs; the defaults are fine to start with.
3. **Read the result.** Click a class. Its selected source opens with highlighting, line numbers and folding. The **View** box at the top switches to any single engine's version or to the bytecode.

![The overview tab after decompiling Gson: whether the result compiles, how many signatures matched, how many classes are exact, and the language and compiler the bytecode points to](images/desktop-overview-dark.png)

What the screen tells you:

- **Confidence level.** Every class carries one: *exact*, *close*, *per file*, *partial* or *unverified* (see [section 6](#6-understanding-the-result)). It appears in the tree, above the editor and in the inspector on the right.
- **Round-trip dots.** In the selected source, each method has a dot in the margin: green when its recompiled body is identical or equivalent to the original, other colors when it differs. javac errors are underlined.
- **Obfuscation banner.** When the bytecode points to a known obfuscator, a banner names it with its evidence. For Skidfuscator and Aidsfuscator, ClassRevive can reverse the jar before decompiling.

Useful keys:

| Key | Action |
|---|---|
| F5 | Decompile |
| Ctrl+N | Go to a class by name |
| Ctrl+F / Ctrl+Shift+F | Find in the current file / search all code |
| Ctrl+click, Alt+Left / Alt+Right | Open the class under the mouse, go back and forward |
| Ctrl+D | Compare two engines side by side |
| Alt+F7 | Find usages of the class, method or field under the caret |
| Ctrl+Alt+H | Call hierarchy of a method |
| Ctrl+, | Settings: theme (dark or light), language (English or Portuguese), font size, default engines, time limit, results folder |

![Two engines' versions of the same Gson class side by side in the comparison view](images/desktop-compare-light.png)

Each decompile writes a new folder under the results folder (by default `%APPDATA%\ClassRevive\workspaces` on Windows), with the same layout as the command line below. **Open result…** reopens any such folder, and **Export project…** saves the sources as an IDE project or a zip.

## 5. The command line

Suppose you want to decompile `Downloads/program.jar`:

```bash
bin/classrevive decompile ~/Downloads/program.jar --output ~/Downloads/program-decompiled --engines all
```

On Windows:

```powershell
bin\classrevive.bat decompile "$HOME\Downloads\program.jar" --output "$HOME\Downloads\program-decompiled" --engines all
```

| Part | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `decompile` | what you want to do |
| `program.jar` | the input file (`.jar`, `.class`, `.apk`, `.dex` or an `.exe` that carries a jar) |
| `--output ...` | where to put the result. **It must be a folder that does not exist yet**; ClassRevive creates it. Without `--output`, it creates `program-classrevive` in the current folder |
| `--engines all` | use all four decompilers. Without it, only CFR and Vineflower run, which is faster but usually gives a worse result |

Paths with spaces need quotes. A small jar takes some tens of seconds; a big one (thousands of classes) can take several minutes.

## 6. Understanding the result

### The summary line

At the end the command prints something like this:

```text
Selected: recompose-1 | compilation=COMPILED | signatures=478/479 | placeholder-signals=1
Sources: selection/sources. Behavior not verified; see selection/selection.txt for evidence.
```

| Part | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `compilation=COMPILED` | **The generated code compiles.** This is the main sign of success. `COMPILE_FAILED` means part of the code has errors |
| `signatures=478/479` | Of the program's 479 pieces of structure (classes, methods, fields), 478 came back with exactly the original shape. The closer to the total, the better |
| `placeholder-signals=1` | Places that look like holes a decompiler left. Sometimes a false alarm: a `throw new UnsupportedOperationException(...)` the original author wrote also counts |
| `Behavior not verified` | An honest reminder: compiling does not prove the program does exactly the same thing |

### Where the code is

The sources are in `program-decompiled/selection/sources/`, in folders by package (for example `org/json/JSONObject.java`). Any editor works; a Java IDE such as IntelliJ IDEA Community or VS Code with the Java extension makes reading much easier.

`program-decompiled/project/` is a **ready-made project**: the code in `src/main/java`, the jar's resources in `src/main/resources`, the libraries you passed with `--classpath` in `lib/`, and a `build.gradle`. Open that folder in your IDE and import it as a Gradle project.

### How much to trust each class

Open `program-decompiled/report.html` in a browser. It is a **confidence map** with a color per class:

| Level | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **exact** (green) | every method came back identical or equivalent to the original |
| **close** (light green) | it compiles, but some methods differ |
| **per file** (blue) | the whole program does not compile, but this class's file does |
| **partial** (orange) | parts of the structure are missing |
| **unverified** (red) | it could not be checked because the file has errors |

### Everything else in the folder

| Path | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `selection/sources/` | **the final result**: the best code chosen |
| `project/` | the same code as an IDE project |
| `report.html` | the confidence map |
| `report.txt` | a text summary of what happened |
| `report.json` | the same with every detail, for scripts ([format](reports.md)) |
| `selection/selection.txt` | the selection log: what each decompiler achieved and what was repaired |
| `cfr/`, `vineflower/`, `procyon/`, `jadx/` | each decompiler's raw output |
| `fallback/bytecode/` | a readable listing of the original instructions, for anything that did not decompile |
| `input.jar`, `classes.jar` | copies of the input used during the run |

### Exit codes (for scripts)

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `0` | everything checked out: it compiles with every signature and no placeholder signals |
| `1` | finished with something partial: missing signatures, placeholder signals or compile errors. **This is the most common case, and the code can still be very good**; look at the `Selected:` line |
| `2` | the command was typed wrong |
| `130` | interrupted (Ctrl+C) |

## 7. When the program depends on other libraries

Most programs use third-party libraries that are not inside the jar you decompile. Without them the recompilation check cannot compile everything. ClassRevive then infers stand-ins for the missing types so the result can still be checked, and marks it **stub-backed**: its signatures were compared against guesses, not the real library. `report.json` lists what was missing:

```text
missing packages (supply with --classpath): org.tukaani.xz (27), ...
```

If you have those jars, pass them with `--classpath`, separated by `;` on Windows and `:` on macOS and Linux:

```bash
bin/classrevive decompile gson-2.13.1.jar --engines all --classpath error_prone_annotations-2.38.0.jar
```

Jars passed this way are only read by the compiler during the check. They are never executed and do not end up in the result. In the desktop application, add them under **Libraries (optional)** in **Decompile with options…**.

## 8. Common problems

| Message or symptom | What to do |
|---|---|
| `Output already exists` | The `--output` folder already exists. Pick another name; ClassRevive never deletes earlier results |
| `java` is not recognized | The JDK 21 is not installed, or the terminal was opened before the installation. See section 2 |
| `compilation=WORKER_FAILED` | The compiler did not run. Check with `javac -version` that a JDK 21 is installed; a JRE is not enough |
| Very slow, or `TIMED_OUT` | Raise the limit per step, in seconds: `--timeout-seconds 600` (default 120, maximum 3600) |
| `UNSUPPORTED_RELEASE` | The program was built for Java 22 or newer; its recompilation cannot be checked yet. |
| `compilation=COMPILE_FAILED` | Part of the code did not compile. See section 7 (missing libraries). The files with problems are listed in `selection/selection.txt`, and the code is still in `selection/sources/` for reading |

## 9. Other useful commands

| Command | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `classrevive inspect file.jar` | list what is inside (each class and the Java version it targets) without decompiling |
| `classrevive identify file.exe` | say what a file is and whether it holds Java |
| `classrevive diagnose file.jar` | static triage: obfuscation techniques, reflection, class loading, crypto |
| `classrevive engines` | list the decompilers and their versions |
| `classrevive --help` | list every command; `classrevive help <command>` explains one |

The advanced commands (`transform`, `rename`, `benchmark`, `lab`) are described in the [command-line reference](cli-reference.md).

## 10. Glossary

- **`.class`**: one compiled Java class.
- **`.jar`**: a zip with many `.class` files, and sometimes images and configuration.
- **Decompiler**: a program that goes back from `.class` to `.java`.
- **Compile**: turn `.java` into `.class`. ClassRevive recompiles its result to check it.
- **Signature**: the shape of a class, method or field: its name, parameters, type and modifiers.
- **Round trip**: recompiling a decompiled method and comparing it with the original, instruction by instruction. When they match, the method came back faithfully.
- **Obfuscation**: deliberately scrambling a program to make it harder to read, for example by renaming everything to short meaningless names. ClassRevive detects common obfuscation and reverses some of it, but it cannot recover renamed names without the obfuscator's mapping file.

```

`docs/guia-iniciante.md`:

```md
# Guia para iniciantes: como descompilar um programa Java com o ClassRevive

Este guia é para quem nunca descompilou nada. Ele mostra como instalar o ClassRevive, descompilar um `.jar` no aplicativo desktop ou na linha de comando e entender o resultado. A versão em inglês está em [getting-started.md](getting-started.md).

## 1. O que é descompilar

Um programa Java costuma ser distribuído compilado: em vez dos arquivos `.java` que o programador escreveu, você recebe arquivos `.class`, geralmente juntos dentro de um `.jar`. Esses arquivos são para a máquina virtual Java, não para pessoas. **Descompilar** é o caminho de volta: transformar `.class` e `.jar` em código `.java` legível de novo.

O ClassRevive não descompila sozinho. Ele roda **quatro descompiladores conhecidos** (CFR, Vineflower, Procyon e JADX), compara os resultados e fica com o melhor, arquivo por arquivo e até método por método. Depois, **confere** o resultado: recompila o código gerado e compara com o bytecode original.

| Faz | Não faz |
|---|---|
| Gera código `.java` a partir de `.jar`, `.class`, `.apk` do Android ou um `.exe` com um jar dentro | Não recupera comentários, formatação nem a maioria dos nomes de variáveis locais; a compilação apagou isso |
| Testa se o código gerado compila de novo | Não prova que o programa se comporta igual ao original |
| Diz quantos métodos voltaram idênticos ou equivalentes ao original | Não executa o programa analisado (isso é proposital, por segurança) |
| Lê arquivos `.class` de qualquer versão do Java até a 28 | Não recompila nem confere arquivos feitos para Java 22 ou mais novo |

> **Só descompile programas que você tem o direito de analisar**: seu próprio código, código aberto, ou casos que a licença ou a lei permitem. Veja o [aviso legal](../DISCLAIMER.md) (em inglês).

## 2. O que você precisa ter instalado

Só uma coisa: o **JDK do Java 21**.

1. Baixe o **Eclipse Temurin 21 (JDK)** em [adoptium.net](https://adoptium.net) para o seu sistema (no Windows, o instalador `.msi`).
2. Instale com as opções padrão. No Windows, se aparecer a opção **Set JAVA_HOME variable**, marque.
3. Confira: abra um terminal (PowerShell no Windows, Terminal no macOS ou no Linux) e rode:

   ```bash
   java -version
   ```

   Deve aparecer algo com `21`, por exemplo `openjdk version "21.0.12"`. Se o comando não for reconhecido, feche e abra o terminal de novo; se continuar, reinstale marcando a opção de PATH/JAVA_HOME.

> Precisa ser o **JDK**, não só o JRE: o ClassRevive usa o compilador Java para conferir o resultado.

## 3. Baixar o ClassRevive

Baixe o zip da versão mais recente na [página de Releases](https://github.com/t1zzo/classrevive/releases) e descompacte numa pasta à sua escolha, por exemplo `Documentos\classrevive` no Windows ou `~/classrevive` no macOS e no Linux. Dentro dela você encontra:

| Pasta | Conteúdo |
|---|---|
| `bin/` | os atalhos para abrir: `classrevive-gui` (aplicativo desktop) e `classrevive` (linha de comando), com versões `.bat` para Windows |
| `lib/` | o programa e os descompiladores que ele usa |
| `docs/` | esta documentação |
| `third-party-licenses/` | as licenças das bibliotecas incluídas |

Para conferir que funciona, abra um terminal nessa pasta e rode:

```bash
bin/classrevive engines
```

No Windows, escreva `bin\classrevive.bat engines`. Devem aparecer os quatro descompiladores (`cfr`, `vineflower`, `procyon`, `jadx`) com as versões.

<details>
<summary>Ou montar a partir do código-fonte</summary>

Com o JDK 21 e uma cópia do repositório, rode `./gradlew :cli:installDist` (`.\gradlew.bat :cli:installDist` no Windows). Na primeira vez isso baixa as dependências e demora alguns minutos. Os atalhos ficam em `modules/cli/build/install/classrevive/bin/`. Veja a [referência da linha de comando](cli-reference.md#build-from-source) (em inglês).

</details>

## 4. O aplicativo desktop

Abra `bin/classrevive-gui` (no Windows, dê dois cliques em `bin\classrevive-gui.bat`). O idioma segue o do sistema e pode ser trocado em **Configurações** (Ctrl+,).

1. **Abra um arquivo.** Use **Abrir arquivo…** ou arraste um `.jar`, `.class`, `.apk` ou `.exe` para a janela. O explorador à esquerda mostra na hora os pacotes, as classes e os recursos; dá para ler o bytecode de qualquer classe antes de descompilar.
2. **Descompile.** Aperte **F5** (ou o botão laranja **Descompilar**). O painel de atividade, embaixo, mostra cada etapa ao vivo, e o botão de parar cancela. **Descompilar com opções…** deixa escolher os descompiladores, o limite de tempo e as bibliotecas de que o programa precisa; os padrões servem para começar.
3. **Leia o resultado.** Clique numa classe. O código escolhido abre com cores, números de linha e dobras. A caixa **Visão**, em cima, troca para a versão de um descompilador específico ou para o bytecode.

O que a tela mostra:

- **Nível de confiança.** Toda classe tem um: *Exata*, *Próxima*, *Por arquivo*, *Parcial* ou *Não verificada* (veja a [seção 6](#6-entendendo-o-resultado)). Ele aparece na árvore, acima do editor e no inspetor à direita.
- **Bolinhas de ida e volta.** No código escolhido, cada método tem uma bolinha na margem: verde quando o corpo recompilado é idêntico ou equivalente ao original, outras cores quando é diferente. Erros do javac aparecem sublinhados.
- **Faixa de ofuscação.** Quando o bytecode aponta para um ofuscador conhecido, uma faixa diz qual, com as evidências. Para Skidfuscator e Aidsfuscator, o ClassRevive pode desfazer a ofuscação antes de descompilar.

Atalhos úteis:

| Tecla | Ação |
|---|---|
| F5 | Descompilar |
| Ctrl+N | Ir para uma classe pelo nome |
| Ctrl+F / Ctrl+Shift+F | Procurar no arquivo atual / pesquisar em todo o código |
| Ctrl+clique, Alt+Esquerda / Alt+Direita | Abrir a classe sob o mouse, voltar e avançar |
| Ctrl+D | Comparar dois descompiladores lado a lado |
| Alt+F7 | Encontrar os usos da classe, do método ou do campo sob o cursor |
| Ctrl+Alt+H | Hierarquia de chamadas de um método |
| Ctrl+, | Configurações: tema (escuro ou claro), idioma (português ou inglês), tamanho da fonte, descompiladores padrão, limite de tempo, pasta de resultados |

Cada descompilação grava uma pasta nova dentro da pasta de resultados (no Windows, por padrão, `%APPDATA%\ClassRevive\workspaces`), com a mesma organização da linha de comando abaixo. **Abrir resultado…** reabre qualquer uma dessas pastas, e **Exportar projeto…** salva o código como projeto de IDE ou como zip.

## 5. A linha de comando

Suponha que você quer descompilar `Downloads/programa.jar`:

```bash
bin/classrevive decompile ~/Downloads/programa.jar --output ~/Downloads/programa-descompilado --engines all
```

No Windows:

```powershell
bin\classrevive.bat decompile "$HOME\Downloads\programa.jar" --output "$HOME\Downloads\programa-descompilado" --engines all
```

| Parte | Significado |
|---|---|
| `decompile` | o que você quer fazer |
| `programa.jar` | o arquivo de entrada (`.jar`, `.class`, `.apk`, `.dex` ou um `.exe` com um jar dentro) |
| `--output ...` | onde guardar o resultado. **Tem que ser uma pasta que ainda não existe**; o ClassRevive cria. Sem `--output`, ele cria `programa-classrevive` na pasta atual |
| `--engines all` | usar os quatro descompiladores. Sem isso ele usa só CFR e Vineflower, que é mais rápido mas costuma dar resultado pior |

Caminhos com espaço precisam de aspas. Um `.jar` pequeno leva algumas dezenas de segundos; um grande (milhares de classes) pode levar vários minutos.

## 6. Entendendo o resultado

### A linha de resumo

No fim, o comando mostra algo assim:

```text
Selected: recompose-1 | compilation=COMPILED | signatures=478/479 | placeholder-signals=1
Sources: selection/sources. Behavior not verified; see selection/selection.txt for evidence.
```

| Trecho | Em português |
|---|---|
| `compilation=COMPILED` | **O código gerado compila.** É o principal sinal de sucesso. `COMPILE_FAILED` quer dizer que parte do código tem erros |
| `signatures=478/479` | Das 479 peças de estrutura do programa (classes, métodos, campos), 478 voltaram com o formato exato do original. Quanto mais perto do total, melhor |
| `placeholder-signals=1` | Trechos que parecem "buracos" deixados por um descompilador. Às vezes é alarme falso: um `throw new UnsupportedOperationException(...)` escrito pelo próprio autor do programa também conta |
| `Behavior not verified` | Lembrete honesto: compilar não prova que o programa faz exatamente a mesma coisa |

### Onde está o código

O código fica em `programa-descompilado/selection/sources/`, em pastas por pacote (por exemplo `org/json/JSONObject.java`). Qualquer editor serve; uma IDE Java, como o IntelliJ IDEA Community ou o VS Code com a extensão Java, deixa a leitura bem mais fácil.

A pasta `programa-descompilado/project/` é um **projeto pronto**: o código em `src/main/java`, os recursos do jar em `src/main/resources`, as bibliotecas passadas com `--classpath` em `lib/` e um `build.gradle`. Abra essa pasta na IDE e importe como projeto Gradle.

### O quanto confiar em cada classe

Abra `programa-descompilado/report.html` no navegador. É um **mapa de confiança**, com uma cor por classe:

| Nível | Significado |
|---|---|
| **exact** (verde) | todos os métodos voltaram idênticos ou equivalentes ao original |
| **close** (verde-claro) | compila, mas alguns métodos ficaram diferentes |
| **per file** (azul) | o programa inteiro não compila, mas o arquivo dessa classe sim |
| **partial** (laranja) | faltam partes da estrutura |
| **unverified** (vermelho) | não deu para conferir, porque o arquivo tem erros |

### As outras coisas na pasta

| Caminho | Para que serve |
|---|---|
| `selection/sources/` | **o resultado final**: o melhor código escolhido |
| `project/` | o mesmo código como projeto de IDE |
| `report.html` | o mapa de confiança |
| `report.txt` | resumo em texto do que aconteceu |
| `report.json` | o mesmo, com todos os detalhes, para scripts ([formato](reports.md), em inglês) |
| `selection/selection.txt` | o diário da escolha: o que cada descompilador conseguiu e o que foi consertado |
| `cfr/`, `vineflower/`, `procyon/`, `jadx/` | o resultado bruto de cada descompilador |
| `fallback/bytecode/` | uma listagem legível das instruções originais, para o que não descompilou |
| `input.jar`, `classes.jar` | cópias da entrada usadas no processo |

### O código de saída (para quem usa scripts)

| Código | Significa |
|---|---|
| `0` | tudo conferido: compila com todas as assinaturas e sem sinais de "buraco" |
| `1` | terminou com algo parcial: assinaturas faltando, sinais de "buraco" ou erros de compilação. **É o caso mais comum, e o código pode estar ótimo mesmo assim**; olhe a linha `Selected:` |
| `2` | comando digitado errado |
| `130` | interrompido (Ctrl+C) |

## 7. Quando o programa depende de outras bibliotecas

A maioria dos programas usa bibliotecas de terceiros que não estão dentro do jar que você descompila. Sem elas, a conferência não consegue compilar tudo. O ClassRevive então deduz substitutos para os tipos que faltam, para ainda conseguir conferir o resultado, e o marca como **stub-backed**: as assinaturas foram comparadas com palpites, não com a biblioteca de verdade. O `report.json` lista o que faltou:

```text
missing packages (supply with --classpath): org.tukaani.xz (27), ...
```

Se você tiver esses jars, passe com `--classpath`, separados por `;` no Windows e por `:` no macOS e no Linux:

```bash
bin/classrevive decompile gson-2.13.1.jar --engines all --classpath error_prone_annotations-2.38.0.jar
```

Os jars passados assim só são lidos pelo compilador durante a conferência. Eles nunca são executados e não entram no resultado. No aplicativo desktop, adicione em **Bibliotecas (opcional)**, dentro de **Descompilar com opções…**.

## 8. Problemas comuns

| Mensagem ou sintoma | O que fazer |
|---|---|
| `Output already exists` | A pasta de `--output` já existe. Escolha outro nome; o ClassRevive nunca apaga resultados antigos |
| `java` não é reconhecido | O JDK 21 não está instalado, ou o terminal foi aberto antes da instalação. Veja a seção 2 |
| `compilation=WORKER_FAILED` | O compilador não rodou. Confira com `javac -version` se o JDK 21 está instalado; só o JRE não basta |
| Demora demais ou `TIMED_OUT` | Aumente o limite por etapa, em segundos: `--timeout-seconds 600` (o padrão é 120, o máximo 3600) |
| `UNSUPPORTED_RELEASE` | O programa foi feito para Java 22 ou mais novo; a recompilação dele ainda não pode ser conferida |
| `compilation=COMPILE_FAILED` | Parte do código não compilou. Veja a seção 7 (bibliotecas faltando). Os arquivos com problema aparecem em `selection/selection.txt`, e o código continua em `selection/sources/` para leitura |

## 9. Outros comandos úteis

| Comando | Para que serve |
|---|---|
| `classrevive inspect arquivo.jar` | mostra o que tem dentro (cada classe e a versão do Java para a qual foi feita), sem descompilar |
| `classrevive identify arquivo.exe` | diz o que é um arquivo e se ele tem Java dentro |
| `classrevive diagnose arquivo.jar` | triagem estática: técnicas de ofuscação, reflexão, carregamento de classes, criptografia |
| `classrevive engines` | lista os descompiladores e as versões |
| `classrevive --help` | lista todos os comandos; `classrevive help <comando>` explica um deles |

Os comandos avançados (`transform`, `rename`, `benchmark`, `lab`) estão na [referência da linha de comando](cli-reference.md) (em inglês).

## 10. Glossário rápido

- **`.class`**: um arquivo compilado de Java (uma classe).
- **`.jar`**: um zip com vários `.class` e, às vezes, imagens e configurações.
- **Descompilador**: programa que faz o caminho de volta, de `.class` para `.java`.
- **Compilar**: transformar `.java` em `.class`. O ClassRevive recompila o resultado para conferir se está certo.
- **Assinatura**: o formato de uma classe, de um método ou de um campo: nome, parâmetros, tipo e modificadores.
- **Ida e volta (round trip)**: recompilar um método descompilado e comparar com o original, instrução por instrução. Se bate, o método voltou fiel.
- **Ofuscação**: embaralhar um programa de propósito para dificultar a leitura, por exemplo trocando todos os nomes por nomes curtos e sem sentido. O ClassRevive detecta ofuscações comuns e desfaz algumas, mas não consegue recuperar nomes trocados sem o arquivo de mapeamento do ofuscador.

```

`docs/obfuscation-detection.md`:

```md
# Static obfuscation detection

ClassRevive recognizes obfuscation techniques by static analysis and suggests which obfuscator the pattern points to. It never runs the analyzed code: ASM parses the class bytes, and no class is defined, loaded or initialized; no bootstrap method or string decryptor is evaluated by the detector. The suggestion is a hypothesis from the documented rules below, never proof. `none` (no technique) and `unknown` (techniques, no matching rule) are valid answers.

The detector is `ObfuscationProfile` (module `bytecode`); the rules that turn a profile into hypotheses are `ObfuscatorClassifier` (same module); the readable and JSON forms are `ObfuscationSummary` (module `pipeline`).

## 1. Detector (`ObfuscationProfile`)

`ObfuscationProfile.Builder` takes class bytes (`addClass`) and resource names and sizes (`addResource`; a resource is never read). `build()` applies each technique's threshold. Detected techniques have a class count, an occurrence count and up to 10 samples (class, method and descriptor). Every raw indicator stays in `indicators`, detected or not.

String literal contents are never reported. The only literal values that reach a report are cipher algorithm names from a fixed list (`DES`, `DESede`, `AES`, `Blowfish`, `RC4`, ...) and the fixed word `ALLATORI`.

| Technique | Counted when | Detected when |
|---|---|---|
| `STRING_ENCRYPTION` | a `<clinit>` that calls JCE (`Cipher`, `SecretKeyFactory`, `KeyGenerator`, `javax/crypto/spec`) or XORs, and stores into a static `String`/`String[]` field; a **decryptor**: a static method returning `String`, with 1–4 parameters of type `I J S B C String Object char[] byte[]`, that XORs or calls JCE and builds a string (`new String`, `toCharArray`, `charAt`, `valueOf`, `intern`) or reads a static `String[]`; calls to decryptors, except calls from a bootstrap or call-site handler (first parameter `MethodHandles.Lookup`), which only forward (`strings.decryptor_forwarding_calls`); **invokedynamic sites** whose descriptor is `(...)Ljava/lang/String;` and equals the descriptor of a decoder that the site's bootstrap reaches (see `CONSTANT_ENCRYPTION`); Skidfuscator's seed-keyed decryptor sites | a `<clinit>` decryption, 3 decryptor calls with a literal argument, 3 calls to a decryptor whose parameters are all primitive (`(IJ)`, `(II)`), or 3 invokedynamic sites whose bootstrap reaches a decoder. A `(String)String` helper such as a case-conversion utility also XORs and builds strings; it counts only with literal arguments |
| `CONSTANT_ENCRYPTION` | invokedynamic sites with descriptor `(...)I` or `(...)J` equal to the descriptor of a decoder that the site's bootstrap reaches. A **decoder** is a static method with 1–4 `I J S B C` parameters, returning `String`, `int` or `long`, that XORs or calls JCE; the bootstrap (`(Lookup, String, MethodType...)`) **reaches** it through static calls and `ldc` method handles inside its own class, at most 3 steps (for example bootstrap → `ldc` handler `(Lookup, MutableCallSite, String, Object[])` → decoder `a(IJ)`) | 3 sites. Indicators `constants.indy_int_sites`, `constants.indy_long_sites` |
| `HIDDEN_CALLS` | invokedynamic whose bootstrap owner is outside the JDK (`java/`, `javax/`, `jdk/`, `sun/`, `com/sun/`) and outside language runtimes (Groovy, Scala, Kotlin, Clojure, JRuby); lambdas and string concatenation are never counted. Encrypted-value sites are hidden calls too | any site. Indicators: bootstrap shape `(Lookup, String, MethodType)` exactly or with extra parameters, and whether the owner is a class of the jar |
| `SHORT_NAMES` | a class whose own simple name has at most 2 characters (anonymous `$1` excluded), or with at least 3 members of which 60% have at most 2 characters | at least 5 classes and 10% of the classes |
| `NON_IDENTIFIER_NAMES` | a class name segment, method or field name that is no Java identifier or is a reserved word. Excluded: local classes (`Outer$1Local`), `package-info`/`module-info`, Kotlin's mangled names (`constructor-impl`, `getValue-UwyO8pc`, also with a `$suffix` after the hash), and Java keywords used as member names in a class carrying `kotlin.Metadata` | any |
| `CASE_COLLISIONS` | class names equal ignoring case (`app/A`, `app/a`) | any group |
| `STRIPPED_ATTRIBUTES` | a `$` class without `InnerClasses` (and without `NestHost`), a class without `SourceFile`, a class with code but no `LineNumberTable` | a stripped `InnerClasses`, or `SourceFile` or `LineNumberTable` missing from half the classes. `javac -g:none` also strips the latter two, so this alone is no obfuscator evidence. A missing `LocalVariableTable` is only an indicator: javac omits it by default |
| `EXCEPTION_OBFUSCATION` | an exception handler whose first instruction is `invokestatic` of a `(LX;)LX;` method followed by `athrow`, where that method is a static identity helper of the class set (`aload_0; areturn`). javac always stores the caught exception first (`astore`), even for `catch (E e) { throw wrap(e); }` | 10 handlers in 2 classes |
| `NATIVE_LAYER` | a native method whose name is no identifier or is 16+ hex digits; a known native-obfuscator loader (`native0/Loader`, `JNIC*`); bundled `.dll`/`.so`/`.dylib`/`.jnilib` (indicator) | an obfuscated native name or a loader. Ordinary JNI bindings (identifier names) beside a bundled library are not a protection layer |
| `CONTROL_FLOW` | conditional jumps on constants (`ICONST_1; IFEQ`) with no jump target between the constant and the test; switch dispatch loops (a switch with at least 4 cases that at least 4 later `GOTO`s jump back to); methods with at least 30 instructions of which a quarter are `GOTO`, not counting forward gotos to a label that at least three forward gotos share; a static flag of the class loaded into a local at method entry (in at least a third of a class's methods); a **flag accessor** (a static `()[X`/`()Z`/`()I` method of the class set whose body is `getstatic; return`) whose result is stored in a local that is only ever loaded straight into `ifnull`/`ifnonnull` (array) or `ifeq`/`ifne` (`Z`/`I`); Skidfuscator's self-looping hash switches | 3 constant conditions, 2 dispatch loops, 3 goto-heavy methods, 3 flag classes, or flag-accessor locals in 10 methods of 3 classes. `GOTO` chains (a `GOTO` to a `GOTO`) are only an indicator: javac emits them too, for `finally` and try-with-resources exits |

The two exclusions in `CONTROL_FLOW` keep compiler output out: a materialized boolean (`iload x; ifeq Z; iconst_1; goto M; Z: iconst_0; M: ifeq ...`, as kotlinc writes it) reaches the test through the merge label `M`, and a `when`/`switch` expression with many arms compiles to one `goto exit` per arm, all to the same label.

Other indicators feed the classifier:

- `zkm.long_key_methods` (a method XOR-ing a `long` parameter with a `long` constant), `cipher.<ALGORITHM>`, `strings.decryptor(<shape>)`;
- `debug.sourcefile_renamed` (`SourceFile` set to `"SourceFile"` or an `r8-map-id-…`), `names.short_packages`;
- `marker.allatori`, `marker.stringer_stacktrace` (a decryptor that reads the stack trace), `marker.dasho` (references to `com/preemptive/`), `native.load_calls`;
- `strings.indy_sites`, `indy.decoding_bootstraps`, and `strings.native_key_classes`: a class that decodes values, by a decryptor or a decoding bootstrap, while its `<clinit>` is only constants and static calls, at least one of them to a native method of the class (the keys and tables come from native code);
- `cf.flag_accessors`, `cf.flag_accessor_methods`, `cf.flag_accessor_tests`, `cf.flag_accessor_classes`, `exceptions.identity_helpers`, `exceptions.rethrow_handlers`, `exceptions.rethrow_classes`;
- Skidfuscator: `skid.self_loop_hash_switches`, `skid.seed_methods` (methods with at least 3 `seed = C ^ seed` updates), `skid.seed_string_decryptors` and `strings.skid_sites`, `skid.random_seed_fields`, `skid.parseint_seeds`, `skid.exception_gotos`, `marker.skidfuscator_sdk` (`sdk/SDK`), `marker.ahegao` (its `nothing_to_see_here` marker field), `skid.sdk_calls`;
- Aidsfuscator: `aids.salt_dispatcher` (an FNV-1a class-name hash with a salt retriever), `aids.reference_bootstrap` (a `MutableCallSite` bootstrap with an `(int, int)` reference decoder), `aids.hash_integrity` (SHA-256 hashes of the class files read from a `.bin` resource), `aids.stacktrace_string_decryptors`, `aids.lookup_class_retrievers` (`<clinit>` salts read through `MethodHandles.lookup().lookupClass()`).

## 2. Classifier (`ObfuscatorClassifier`)

Each rule adds points for its evidence and subtracts points for evidence pointing elsewhere. The score is bounded to 0..100. A hypothesis is reported from 30 points: `LOW` below 45, `MEDIUM` below 70, `HIGH` from 70. Hypotheses are sorted by score, and every reason carries its points.

| Hypothesis | Points |
|---|---|
| **Zelix KlassMaster** | +25 hidden calls through a jar-owned `(Lookup, String, MethodType)` bootstrap; +25 `(IJ)`/`(JI)` string decryptors; +10 `(II)` decryptors; +20 DES/DESede with `<clinit>` decryption (+10 for another JCE algorithm); +10 three or more long-key methods; +5 static flags at method entry with control-flow obfuscation; +10 flag-accessor opaque predicates in 10 methods; +15 exception obfuscation; +10 int/long constant encryption with a `(Lookup, String, MethodType)` bootstrap; +10 short or case-colliding names (only with other evidence); −30 with an Allatori or Stringer marker. Flag accessors and exception obfuscation together give 25 points, below the reporting threshold: they confirm the hypothesis, they do not suggest it alone |
| **Allatori** | +80 `ALLATORI` marker (names or literals); +25 `(String)String` decryptors called with literals; +5 short names (with the marker); −20 without the marker when `(IJ)` decryptors or `(Lookup, String, MethodType)` bootstraps point to another tool |
| **Stringer** | +50 decryptors reading the stack trace; +20 `(Object)String` decryptors; +15 hidden calls (only with other evidence) |
| **DashO (PreEmptive)** | +70 references to `com/preemptive/`; +10 string encryption (with the marker) |
| **ProGuard / R8 (renaming only)** | +35 short names; +15 five classes in packages whose segments have at most 2 characters (`a/a/a`); +25 renamed `SourceFile`; +5 no `LocalVariableTable` in half the classes; −30 string encryption, −30 hidden calls, −15 non-identifier names (ProGuard and R8 have none of them by default) |
| **custom native protection layer** (or **JNIC / native-obfuscator style** with a known loader) | +40 obfuscated native names; +40 a known loader; +25 bundled native libraries, +10 `System`/`Runtime` `load` calls and +10 decryption keys supplied by the native layer (all three only with other evidence) |
| **Skidfuscator** | +35 two or more self-looping switches on a hash of the seed; +20 seed updates in 3 methods; +15 three seed-keyed decryptor sites; +10 `Random(long).nextInt()` seed fields; +5 `Integer.parseInt("digits")` seeds; +10 caught `throw new X()` gotos (only with other evidence: javac output can contain a few); +25 `sdk/SDK`; +25 `nothing_to_see_here` marker |
| **Aidsfuscator** | +30 salt dispatcher with an FNV-1a class-name hash; +25 `MutableCallSite` reference bootstrap with an `(int, int)` decoder; +20 hash integrity class; +15 two or more stack-trace string decryptors; +10 two or more `lookupClass()` salt reads |

`verdict` is `SUGGESTED` with at least one hypothesis, `NONE` without techniques and hypotheses, `UNKNOWN` otherwise.

## 3. Output

- `diagnose`: `diagnostics.json` gains `obfuscation` (`techniques`, `indicators`, `verdict`, `suggested_obfuscator`, `hypotheses`, `summary`, `interpretation`). The readable form is in `obfuscation.txt` and on the console. The profile is built in the same sandboxed worker as the dynamic linkage scan (`obfuscation.bin`, a bounded format read strictly by the parent) and classified in the parent.
- `decompile`: the profile of the original classes (before portable renames) is built in the parent with ASM, from the bytes read once. `report.txt` gets the readable block before the engine lines, and `report.json` gets `obfuscation`. A Skidfuscator or Aidsfuscator diagnosis with `HIGH` confidence lets `decompile --deobfuscate auto` (the default) run that reversal before the engines.
- The desktop application shows the same summary and hypotheses in its detection view.

The readable block has one line per technique and the suggestion, in this form:

```
Obfuscation (static, N classes):
  string encryption: C classes, S decryption sites (X invokedynamic, Y direct calls, Z <clinit>); keys supplied by the native layer in K classes
  constant encryption (int/long values decrypted at run time): S sites in C classes (I int, L long)
  hidden calls (invokedynamic with a non-JDK bootstrap): S sites in C classes
  ...
Suggested obfuscator: <hypothesis> (<confidence>, <score>/100); ...
```

## 4. How the rules are checked

- `ObfuscationProfileTest` builds every shape with ASM (nothing is loaded): a clean class set gives `NONE`; ZKM-like, Allatori, Stringer, DashO, ProGuard-style, native-layer, Skidfuscator and Aidsfuscator shapes give their hypothesis; javac-shaped and kotlinc-shaped code (materialized booleans, `when` exits, keyword member names, JNI bindings, natives registered without decoding) gives nothing.
- Clean library jars (Apache Commons, Guava, Gson, Ant, ASM, CFR, JNA, zstd-jni, the Kotlin standard library, ...) are expected to give `none`. Each false positive found on such a jar was fixed in the rule, not by an exception for that jar.
- The committed Skidfuscator fixture (`benchmarks/obfuscated/skidfuscator/skid-fixture-obf.jar`) is diagnosed as Skidfuscator with `HIGH` confidence, which is what lets `decompile` reverse it automatically (`AutoDeobfuscationTest`, `ObfuscationCheckTest`).

## 5. Limits

- Every rule is a heuristic on static patterns. Obfuscators share techniques, change between versions and can be chained; a hand-written XOR helper with key parameters can look like a decryptor. Hypotheses are suggestions with their reasons, never proof.
- Rules exist only for the tools listed above. Other tools (Radon, Branchlock, Paramorphism, ...) show up as `UNKNOWN` with their techniques counted.
- Product names are used only to describe the patterns the rules look for; they belong to their owners, and ClassRevive is not affiliated with any of them.
- Control-flow detection is cheap and local (no data-flow analysis). Opaque predicates computed through fields or arithmetic are not recognized; a flag local is followed only when every load of it feeds a test directly.
- Decryption sites are counted, never decrypted, by the detector. Bootstraps that reach a decoder of another class are not followed.
- Indicators are counted over every class, including shaded libraries; samples show which classes they come from.

`docs/pass-sdk.md`:

```md
# Static pass API (experimental v1)

Implement `BytecodePass` with a stable lowercase identifier and `apply(byte[], int)` returning `TransformResult`. Supply trusted pass instances explicitly to `PassPipeline`. No automatic plugin discovery, downloaded code or target classes are loaded. Third-party pass code is executable Java and must be reviewed as trusted tooling; this API is not a sandbox for malicious plugins.

Contract:
- Input/output class bytes are bounded to 16 MiB and total changes to the caller budget.
- A pass must not execute or define target classes, resolve targets through reflection, or perform network requests.
- Every modification must have an audit record attributed to that pass. Zero records requires byte-identical output.
- Return defensive copies; the pipeline clones between stages and rejects oversized output, excess changes and foreign pass IDs.
- Preserve behavior and unknown metadata, or leave the input unchanged. Structural/behavioral validity cannot be established by this interface alone.
- `instructionIndex` is an ASM tree-node index relative to that pass's input. It is not a byte offset or a global original-source location.

The pipeline runs each pass once in the given order; it never repeats until convergence. This bounds orchestration and makes ordering explicit. Pass code itself must bound its work; the shipped CLI additionally uses a timed worker JVM. The change budget is shared across passes and classes. `changeLimitReached` indicates the budget was consumed, not that further opportunities definitely exist.

Example:
```java
var pipeline = new PassPipeline(BuiltinPasses.select("integer-unary,integer-constants"));
TransformResult result = pipeline.apply(classBytes, 1000);
```

CLI:
```bat
classrevive transform sample.jar --output simplified --passes integer-unary,integer-constants,integer-branches
```

Built-ins: `integer-constants` folds adjacent two-integer arithmetic/bitwise/shift operations; `integer-unary` folds INEG/I2B/I2C/I2S on adjacent integer literals using JVM overflow/narrowing rules; `integer-branches` folds adjacent literal operands for unary `IF*` and binary `IF_ICMP*` comparisons. It does not cross labels, frames or debug nodes, and it leaves reference comparisons and annotated instructions unchanged. Branch audit records preserve the comparison opcode, operands and a result of `1` (taken) or `0` (fallthrough). Unary audit records use `left` for the operand and `right=0`. Default remains `integer-constants` for compatibility. Unknown or duplicate names are rejected before creating output.

The opt-in `string-decryptor` uses a separate strict, bounded static interpreter; it supports only the bytecode/JDK subset listed in the [command-line reference](cli-reference.md#static-simplification), not arbitrary decoder methods. These passes do not provide variable-based branch analysis, general control-flow unflattening or behavioral equivalence. An external plugin loading/packaging protocol remains future work.

## Literal-string partial evaluation

Opt-in `string-length` and `string-char-at` resolve exact adjacent literal calls to `java/lang/String.length()I` and `java/lang/String.charAt(I)C`. The evaluator reads parsed string data; it never invokes a method defined by the target. UTF-16 length and code-unit indexing follow the [Java String contract](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/lang/String.html). Supplementary characters occupy two code units. Out-of-range indices remain unchanged, as do instruction annotations, opaque attributes and sequences crossing a label/frame/debug boundary.

```bat
classrevive transform sample.jar --output simplified --passes string-length,string-char-at,integer-unary,integer-constants,integer-branches
```

Distinct audit pass IDs identify the operation. `left` is string length, `right` is 0 for length or the character index, and `result` is the integer output. The literal text is not duplicated into audit logs; original snapshots and constant pools still contain it. This is not a redaction feature. As with other optimizing transformations, exceptional VM resource exhaustion or modified JDK implementations are not modeled. No arbitrary method evaluator is implemented.

```

`docs/releasing.md`:

```md
# Preparing a release

No public release is claimed until a maintainer publishes one. Current artifacts are development builds.

1. Use a clean checkout and JDK 21. Run `gradlew clean build benchmarkFixtures :cli:installDist` (use `./gradlew` on Unix).
2. Run the installed CLI's `benchmark build/benchmark-corpus --output build/release-benchmark --engines all`.
3. Exit 1 can mean a completed comparison with partial cases. Validate its evidence with `python scripts/check_benchmark.py build/release-benchmark`; inspect every regression instead of requiring artificial perfect scores.
4. Review pinned versions, dependency verification metadata and `THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md`. Every distributed dependency needs its applicable license/notice, including transitives.
5. Inspect `modules/cli/build/distributions/classrevive-<version>.zip`. It includes Windows/Unix launchers, dependencies and licenses. Extract the whole directory; do not distribute the launcher alone. JDK 21 must be installed.
6. Test the distribution in the configured OS matrix and publish exact commands, corpus hashes, engine versions and limitations with the release. Local Windows results do not prove Linux/macOS support.

Do not label the project universally compatible, malware-safe, behaviorally equivalent or 100% recovered. Source comments/names and build context may be irrecoverable. Encrypted runtime payloads require different analysis; this CLI does not execute them.

```

`docs/reports.md`:

```md
# Evidence format, schema version 1

All JSON files are UTF-8. Unknown additive fields should be ignored by consumers; incompatible meaning changes require a schema version increment. No wall-clock timestamps or machine-specific absolute input paths are required. Diagnostics can still contain local paths: review before sharing.

## report.json

- `kind`: `decompilation`; `tool_version`; `schema_version`.
- `input_sha256`: original snapshot hash, not normalized JAR hash.
- `environment`: Java version/vendor, OS and architecture.
- `engines[]`: id/version/status, stable `diagnostic_code`, exit code, source file count, elapsed milliseconds and explanatory message. Codes distinguish `NONE`, `NO_SOURCE_FILES`, `ENGINE_EXIT_NONZERO`, `DEADLINE_EXCEEDED`, `OUTPUT_BUDGET_EXCEEDED`, `CANCELLED`, `WORKER_SETUP_FAILED`, `WORKER_START_FAILED`, and `WORKER_RUNTIME_FAILURE`.
- `verification`: status (`COMPILED`, `COMPILE_FAILED`, `UNSUPPORTED_RELEASE`, `WORKER_FAILED`), error count, matched/expected structural signatures, placeholder signals, structurally_complete, detail, and `class_coverage[]` entries with class name, matched/expected signatures, permille coverage and completion flag. This is structural evidence only. The additive `round_trip` object holds per-method body comparison of the recompiled candidate against the decompiled bytes: `measured`, totals `identical`, `equivalent_after_normalization`, `different`, and `classes[]` with the same counts per class. Selection uses these totals only to break ties between candidates that are equal on every structural criterion. `measured: false` means no comparison ran (the candidate did not compile), not a negative result. Selection does not use these counts yet.
- `selected_candidate`, `provenance` (relative source path to engine), `selection_attempts`.
- `source_repairs`: compiler-guided edits in the selected sources (`count`, `edits[]` with file, line, column, diagnostic code, rule, before and after). Repaired files show `+repair` in `provenance`.
- `method_composition` (additive): method bodies in the selected sources taken from another engine's version of their file: `count`, `files`, and `methods[]` with `file`, `class_name`, `method`, `descriptor`, `engine`, `round_trip_in_place` (`IDENTICAL` or `EQUIVALENT_AFTER_NORMALIZATION`, measured when that file was recompiled alone against the original classes) `canonical_type_names` (types the copied body names canonically because the file's imports did not provide them) and `replaced_body`: `COMPILE_ERROR` when the replaced body failed to compile or `ROUND_TRIP_DIFFERENT` when it compiled but its round trip was `DIFFERENT`; `round_trip_in_place_before` (the method's own outcome before, null when the replaced body did not compile), `also_recovered` (lambda or anonymous-class methods of the body that went from `DIFFERENT` to identical or equivalent, as `class.name(descriptor)`) and `body_repairs` (source repair rules applied to the copied body). `body_repairs` may also name `raw-receiver`, `raw-creation`, `erased-argument`, `drop-redundant-cast` or `drop-upcast` (edits that take away `checkcast`s the original does not have), and `engine` may name the engine whose file is the selected one: that method's own body was edited, not copied. Such files show `+methods` in `provenance`; the rest of the file keeps the listed origin. `evidence` is `METHOD_BODIES_FROM_OTHER_ENGINES_ROUND_TRIP_IN_PLACE_BEHAVIOR_NOT_VERIFIED`.
- `fallback`: null if unnecessary; otherwise an engine-result object. Non-null does not imply successful disassembly.
- `class_confidence` (additive): one entry per class with the level `report.html` shows for it, computed by the same code. Each entry has:
  - `class_name`;
  - `file`: the top-level source file;
  - `origin`: its provenance in the selected sources, or `none`;
  - `matched_symbols` and `expected_symbols`;
  - `identical`, `equivalent_after_normalization` and `different`: method bodies, from the whole candidate's round trip or, when it did not compile, the per-file one;
  - `different_methods`: `name(descriptor)`;
  - `level`: `EXACT`, `CLOSE`, `PER_FILE`, `PARTIAL` or `UNVERIFIED`;
  - `methods`: every measured method as `{method: name + descriptor, outcome: IDENTICAL | EQUIVALENT_AFTER_NORMALIZATION | DIFFERENT}`, empty when the class was not recompiled.

  Levels are recompilation evidence, not behavior.

  A result whose selected sources do not compile also has `selection/diagnostics.tsv`: the selected attempt's javac errors, one per line (file relative to `selection/sources`, line, column, `compiler.err.*` code, message), tab separated and escaped like the compiler worker's own file. They are kept out of `report.json` because messages can name target symbols.
- `behavior`: `NOT_VERIFIED`.

Compilation with full structural coverage is not proof of recovered implementation, malware safety or behavioral equivalence. Annotations and generics are not compared; method bodies are compared only by `round_trip`, which is static bytecode evidence, not behavior. Placeholder counts are not a readability score.

## benchmark.json and progress.jsonl

`rows` contains every completed sample/variant attempt, with snapshot hash, input basename, relative report link when available, `total_elapsed_ms`, and status `STRUCTURALLY_COMPLETE`, `PARTIAL` or `FAILED`. Failed rows include an error rather than invented verification metrics. `variants` holds attempted/recompiled/structurally_complete numerators and denominators. `samples` is the corpus size; `attempted` is the row count across variants. `not_measured` lists missing comparisons/metrics explicitly.

Additive fields (`schema_version` stays 1): each row has `original_method_bodies` (method bodies in the normalized input, counted once per case; `null` when no `classes.jar` was produced) and each variant has a `metrics` object that keeps the metrics apart: `compilable` and `structural` (numerator over every attempt, failures included), `method_round_trip`, and `behavioral_equivalence` / `deobfuscation` with `status: NOT_MEASURED` and a reason. `method_round_trip` sums the rows' `verification.round_trip` counts: `measured_attempts`, `identical`, `equivalent_after_normalization`, `different`, `methods_compared`, `recovered_methods` (identical + equivalent) and `recovered_permille` over `methods_compared` (only attempts whose candidate recompiled), plus `corpus_method_bodies` and `recovered_of_corpus_permille`, where attempts that did not recompile count as not recovered (`attempts_without_method_count` are excluded from that denominator). Permille values are rounded down and are `null` with a zero denominator. `different` includes legitimate compiler variation. None of these numbers is an original-source recovery percentage, and selection does not use them.

Each row also lists its `failure_cases` (ids under `failures/`), and `failures` in the report gives the case, signature and category counts with a link to `failures/failures.json`.

`progress.jsonl` contains one completed row per line. It is incremental and may be truncated on abrupt process termination. It is not a completed aggregate or a resume protocol. Deleting an output is never automatic.

## Failure lab files

- `failures/failures.json` (`kind: failure-lab`): `cases`, `signatures`, `categories` (count per category) and `groups[]`, most frequent first. Each group has `signature`, `category`, `engine` (producer), `detail`, `cases`, `selected` (cases in the candidate the job chose), `recoverable_by_other_candidate` (METHOD_DIFFERENT cases where another engine candidate of the same job got the method identical or equivalent), `variants` and `case_ids`. It names no target class, member, constant or path.
- `failures/failure-NNNN/case.json` (`kind: failure-case`): `signature`, `category`, `engine`, `detail`, `engine_version`, `variant`, `sample`, `candidate`, `selected`, `source_repair`, `class_name`, `class_sha256`, `method`, `source_file`, `reason`, `excerpt` (bounded, absolute paths redacted), `alternatives`, `recoverable_by`, `input_sha256` and `context` (a relative path to the job's class JAR, or null). It sits next to `classes.jar`, and `candidate.java` and `recompiled.class` when available. It is target-derived evidence.
- `minimization.json` (`kind: failure-minimization`): `status` (`MINIMIZED`, `BUDGET_EXHAUSTED`, `NOT_REPRODUCIBLE`, `ORIGINAL_DOES_NOT_LINK`, `UNSUPPORTED`), `budget`, `evaluations`, `accepted`, `original`/`minimized` sizes (classes, bytes, members, instructions), `contrast_engines`, `contrast_levels` and `steps[]` (phase, description, outcome `ACCEPTED`/`REJECTED_LINK`/`REJECTED_SIGNATURE`/`REJECTED_NOT_REPEATED`/`REJECTED_CONTRAST`/`REJECTED_ERROR`, detail, time).
- `benchmarks/regressions/<case>/expected.json` (`kind: regression-case`): `variants.<variant>` with `engines`, `source_repair` and `minimum_levels` (method key `class.name(desc)` to `NOT_RECOMPILED`, `DIFFERENT`, `EQUIVALENT_AFTER_NORMALIZATION` or `IDENTICAL`), plus `provenance`, `signature`, `classes_sha256`, `measured_with` and `unstable_at_promotion`. `lab-check` writes `regressions.json` (`kind: regression-check`, `passed`, `checks[]` with verdict `SAME`, `IMPROVED` or `REGRESSED`, and `errors`) and `regressions.md`.

Reproducibility means same corpus bytes, pinned engines and method can be rerun; timings naturally vary. Engine versions and Java environment must match for meaningful comparison. This small authored corpus does not represent arbitrary obfuscators or encrypted loaders.

```

`docs/sandbox.md`:

```md
# Sandbox readiness (experimental)

`classrevive sandbox-check` performs a bounded read-only `docker info` against a fixed local endpoint. It does not start Docker, pull images, create containers, load target classes or execute a target. Exit 1 means unavailable/unsupported; exit 0 means only that a Linux daemon answered. `AVAILABLE_NOT_VERIFIED` is deliberately not an execution safety guarantee.

Windows probes Docker Desktop's Linux named pipe; Linux/macOS currently probe `/var/run/docker.sock`. Rootless/custom endpoints are not supported yet. Remote Docker contexts and environment endpoint overrides are not used.

The experimental Java policy builder specifies a non-root container, read-only root/input, no network, no capabilities, no-new-privileges, fixed local image ID, no image pull, CPU/memory/process limits and bounded tmpfs. It is not wired to execution. It assumes a prepared isolated input folder and a reviewed Temurin-compatible image with `/opt/java/openjdk/bin/java`.

Before enabling behavior comparison, implementation still needs image inspection (including inherited environment/volumes), prepared input validation, real containment conformance tests, bounded output capture, timeout/container cleanup, and a test/result comparison protocol. Container policy is not protection against all kernel/runtime vulnerabilities; hostile samples require a disposable isolated environment.

Local evidence on 2026-10-15: Docker CLI installed; Linux daemon pipe absent. No target was executed, and no host-execution fallback was attempted. Behavioral equivalence remains NOT_VERIFIED.

The [behavior protocol](behavior-protocol.md) defines immutable paired observations and conservative comparison statuses. It is implemented separately from execution and cannot itself establish that containment or actual tests occurred.

Reference: https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/container/run/

```

`docs/status.md`:

```md
# Status: what works and what remains

This page lists ClassRevive's capabilities with the evidence behind them and the work that remains. Nothing here claims universal recovery of original source: obfuscation, missing dependencies and information discarded by compilation can prevent a faithful reconstruction. For numbers, see [benchmarks](benchmarks.md), which also explains how to run the scoreboard yourself.

| Area | What works today (evidence) | Remaining work |
|---|---|---|
| Engines and selection | CFR, Vineflower, Procyon and JADX run as separate JVM workers with stable outcome codes. Candidates are ranked by recompilation, structural signature coverage (each class weighted equally), javac errors, per-method round trip and placeholder signals. Bounded hybrids mix files guided by javac's per-file errors; bounded source repairs fix common decompiler errors; per-method composition takes a method body from another engine only when it recompiles and its round trip is identical or equivalent (tests, benchmark corpus, scoreboard) | Exhaustive search is not attempted; behavioral equivalence is not verified |
| Recompilation and round trip | javac in a worker with `-proc:none`, an empty source path and either an empty class path or explicit local JARs; Java 1.1..21 inputs (1.1..7 with `--release 8`); per-method bytecode round trip with normalizations for javac variations and decompiler rewritings that keep JVM semantics; inferred stubs for missing libraries, with stub-backed results marked as such | Java 22+ inputs report `UNSUPPORTED_RELEASE` under JDK 21; generic signatures, annotations and constant values are not compared |
| Readable fallback | ASM dump of the original instructions when recovery is partial; ASM 9.11.1 parses class versions through Java 28 | — |
| Static simplification | Opt-in, bounded passes: integer constant and branch folding (output passes the JVM verifier), adjacent string operations, and a static interpreter for pure single-`String` decoder methods with an explicit allowlist and time/memory budgets (see [pass API](pass-sdk.md)) | Broader opcode and data-flow patterns, each with authored regression fixtures |
| Obfuscation detection | Static technique profile and obfuscator hypotheses with scores and reasons (see [obfuscation detection](obfuscation-detection.md)); clean library jars give `none` | Rules for more tools; data-flow based opaque predicates |
| Obfuscator reversal | Skidfuscator and Aidsfuscator reversals (whole-jar passes, checked by the JVM verifier without initializing classes), applied automatically by `decompile` on a `HIGH` diagnosis; ZKM opaque-predicate flags proved constant over the whole jar are folded | Renamed names cannot be recovered without a mapping; other obfuscators are detected, not reversed |
| Renaming | Deterministic aliases or explicit mapping files for class sets, private members, manifests, `META-INF/services` and literal reflection calls; ProGuard/R8 mapping import restricted to what can be applied safely, with per-reason skip evidence; portable names for case-colliding classes and non-identifier member names before decompiling | Public/virtual member renaming needs hierarchy-aware analysis; reflection through variables is not followed |
| Inputs | `.class`, `.jar`, multi-release jars (base version), executables with an embedded jar, bundles of jars, Android APK/dex (converted by dex2jar in a worker), with input identification from the bytes | App bundles (`.aab`) and split-APK sets are identified, not converted |
| Diagnostics | Static invokedynamic, reflection, class-loading and crypto references (clues only, never a verdict); compiler fingerprint (javac, ecj, Kotlin, Scala, Groovy); embedded library recognition; optional Ghidra triage of bundled native libraries | Reliable packer or encryption identification is not claimed |
| Reports | `report.txt`, `report.json` (schema v1), a self-contained `report.html` confidence map, an IDE project export (see [report format](reports.md)) | Stable public Java API |
| Desktop application | Swing + FlatLaf + RSyntaxTextArea on the same pipeline: browse, decompile with progress and cancel, per-class confidence, per-method round-trip marks, engine comparison, obfuscator banner with reversal, find usages and call hierarchy, search, export, English and Portuguese | Further features are planned separately |
| Benchmarks and failure lab | Authored corpus and ProGuard fixtures; scoreboard on hash-checked Maven Central libraries (`dev`, `holdout`, `holdout2` sets); failure lab that captures, minimizes and promotes regression cases checked by `./gradlew test` | Repeated trials, readability metrics, more obfuscators in the corpus |
| Behavioral verification | Sandbox probe and evidence protocol only; target execution is disabled (see [sandbox](sandbox.md), [behavior protocol](behavior-protocol.md)) | Isolated runner, capture and paired execution; never host execution |
| Extensibility | Engine interface and an experimental pass API with an explicit built-in registry | External plugin packaging and a stable SDK |
| Distribution | `./gradlew :cli:installDist :cli:distZip` (launchers `classrevive` and `classrevive-gui`); requires a Java 21 JDK | Releases with checksums; a runtime image that does not need a separate JDK |

```
